q: An orders API handles 2,000 concurrent requests, each mostly waiting for PostgreSQL. What does Node use while those requests wait?
options: One thread per request, taken from a large internal pool
The libuv thread pool, one of its 4 threads per database query
The operating system's asynchronous socket APIs; the main thread only runs a callback when data arrives
A separate event loop per open connection
explain: Database connections are network sockets, and libuv watches them through epoll, kqueue or IOCP without a thread per connection. The main thread runs a callback only when a socket has data. The thread pool is the tempting answer, but it serves fs, dns.lookup, async crypto and zlib, not sockets: with only 4 threads it could not hold 2,000 waiting queries.

q: In which phase of the event loop do setImmediate callbacks run?
options: The timers phase, right after the timeouts that are due
The check phase, right after the poll phase
The poll phase, together with I/O callbacks
Before the loop starts, like process.nextTick
explain: setImmediate callbacks have their own phase, check, which comes right after poll. That is why "immediate" really means "after this round of I/O". process.nextTick is not a phase at all: its queue is drained after every callback.

q: This file is CommonJS (order.cjs). What does it print?
options: A F D E, then B and C
A F E D B C, always in that order
A E D F B C
A F E D, then B and C in an order that is not guaranteed
explain: Synchronous code runs first (A, F), then the nextTick queue (E), then promise microtasks (D). From the main module, whether the 1 ms timer is due when the loop first reaches timers depends on startup time: measured on Node 24, C came first in 26 runs out of 30. A F D E is the ES module order, not the CommonJS one.

q: Inside the callback of fs.readFile, you schedule setTimeout(f, 0) and setImmediate(g). Which runs first?
options: g, every time, because the check phase comes right after poll
f, every time, because its delay is the shortest
Either one, depending on how busy the machine is
f, because timers always run before check
explain: The readFile callback runs in the poll phase. The next phase is check, so setImmediate runs before the loop wraps around to timers (10 runs out of 10 measured). The "either order" answer is true only at the top level of the main module.

q: Which of these operations waits for a libuv thread pool thread?
options: Reading the body of an incoming HTTP request
A query sent over an open PostgreSQL connection
A setTimeout(fn, 100) callback
fs.promises.readFile('./invoice.pdf')
explain: File system calls, in callback or promise style, run on the thread pool because there is no portable asynchronous file API. Request bodies and database queries travel over sockets, which use the OS asynchronous APIs, and timers live in the loop itself.

q: What is true about the libuv thread pool size?
options: It equals the number of CPU cores, detected at startup
It is 4 by default and is set with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable when the process starts
It grows on demand up to 1024 threads
It is 4 per worker thread, so each worker brings its own pool
explain: The default is 4 regardless of cores, and UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (maximum 1024) changes it at startup. The libuv documentation says the pool is global and shared across all event loops, so worker threads share it rather than bringing their own.

q: A handler spends 600 ms of CPU building a report. A colleague makes the builder function async. What changes for the other requests in the same process?
options: Nothing: the 600 ms still run on the main thread and still block them
They are no longer blocked, because async functions run on the thread pool
They are blocked only half as long, because await splits the work
They are no longer blocked, because V8 runs async functions on another core
explain: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, and a CPU loop has nothing to await, so the work stays on the main thread. Measured on Node 24: a 10 ms timer fired after about 400 ms while an async function with no await was computing. The thread pool never runs your JavaScript.

q: An endpoint matches 20,000 orders to 20,000 payments with a nested find and blocks the loop for 3 seconds. What should you try first?
options: Move the matching to a pool of worker threads
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 16
Index the payments in a Map so each lookup is constant time
Put the matching on a BullMQ queue and answer 202
explain: A nested find is quadratic: 400 million comparisons. A Map lookup makes it linear and usually removes the problem entirely, at no operational cost. Workers or a queue would only move 3 seconds of avoidable work elsewhere, and the thread pool never runs JavaScript.

q: Your team runs a Node API on Kubernetes and needs more throughput. What is the usual setup in 2026?
options: One container running PM2 in cluster mode with one process per core
One Node process per container, and more replicas scaled by Kubernetes
One container with the cluster module, plus a worker thread per request
A single large pod with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE raised to the number of cores
explain: With one process per container, Kubernetes restarts crashed processes, balances traffic and sees each process in its metrics. PM2 or cluster inside the container duplicates that work and hides crashes from the orchestrator; they belong to older VM deployments.

q: What does performance.eventLoopUtilization() tell you?
options: The share of time the loop spent running callbacks rather than waiting, between 0 and 1
How many milliseconds late the last timer fired
The CPU usage of the whole process, including the thread pool
The number of callbacks waiting in the poll queue
explain: ELU is the fraction of time the loop was busy. Measured on Node 24: 0.02 idle and 0.96 with constant CPU work. How late timers fire is the other metric, event loop delay, from monitorEventLoopDelay.

q: On Node 24 with default flags, a promise rejects and no code handles it. What happens?
options: A warning is printed and the process keeps running
The rejection is silently ignored
The rejection is retried on the next turn of the loop
The error is printed and the process exits with code 1
explain: Since Node 15 the default mode is --unhandled-rejections=throw: the rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, and with no handler the process exits with code 1 (verified on Node 24). Printing a warning and continuing was the behaviour before Node 15.

q: You run node src/status.ts on Node 24, and the file declares enum OrderStatus { Paid, Open }. What happens?
options: It runs: Node compiles the enum with the TypeScript compiler
It runs, but type errors elsewhere in the file are reported first
It fails with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX, because enum needs code generation
It fails because Node requires a tsconfig.json to run TypeScript
explain: Node only strips erasable types; an enum produces JavaScript, so it fails with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX (verified on Node 24.11). Node never type-checks and ignores tsconfig.json, so neither of the other failure modes exists. Use an as const object or a union type instead.

q: The same six lines are saved as order.mjs, an ES module. What does it print?
options: A F E D, then B and C in either order
A F D E, then B and C in either order
A F D E B C, always
A D E F, then B and C in either order
explain: An ES module body is evaluated inside a promise job, so the microtask queue (D) is drained before Node reaches the nextTick queue (E). Measured on Node 24: A F D E every time, with B and C in either order (7 and 3 out of 10). A F E D is the CommonJS order.

q: In an ES module, a request handler runs this code. In what order do the two lines print?
options: promise, then nextTick, because the file is an ES module
Either order, depending on load
nextTick, then promise
Only nextTick: the promise is dropped when the response ends
explain: Inside any callback Node drains the nextTick queue before the microtask queue, in both module systems. The promise-first order only applies to the top-level body of an ES module, which is itself run as a promise job (verified on Node 24 with the same calls inside a timer callback).

q: The job below takes about 2.7 seconds. How many times does tick print?
options: About 27, one every 100 ms
About 100, one per chunk
It depends on the number of CPU cores
Zero
explain: After await Promise.resolve() the function resumes in a microtask, and microtasks are drained before the loop moves on, so the timers phase is never reached until the job ends, by which time the interval is cleared. Measured on Node 24: 0 ticks, versus 24 with await setImmediate() from node:timers/promises.

q: In what order are the lines printed?
options: timer, sync done, sum done
sync done, timer, sum done
sync done, sum done, timer
sum done, sync done, timer
explain: sumUpTo has no await, so the whole loop runs synchronously before sync done is logged. Its result is delivered in a microtask, which runs before the loop reaches the timers phase, so sum done beats the timer, which fired late (about 400 ms instead of 10, measured). "async" never means "on another thread".

q: On a 16-core server with default settings, you start 8 crypto.pbkdf2 calls at once, each needing about 250 ms of CPU. When does the last one finish?
options: After about 250 ms: there are enough cores for all eight
After about 500 ms: they run in two waves of four
After about 2 seconds: they run one by one on the main thread
After about 250 ms, but the main thread is blocked meanwhile
explain: Asynchronous pbkdf2 runs on the libuv pool, which has 4 threads regardless of cores, so eight jobs run in two waves (measured on Node 24: four finished together, the other four about one hash-duration later). With UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 all eight finished together. The main thread stays free throughout.

q: During login peaks (asynchronous password hashing), calls to a partner API by hostname become slow, while CPU sits at 40%. The partner says its latency is normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hashes block the main thread, so responses are read late
The partner API rate-limits you during your peaks
fetch opens a new thread per call and the OS runs out of threads
fetch resolves the hostname with dns.lookup, which queues on the thread pool behind the hashes
explain: Asynchronous pbkdf2 or scrypt occupy the 4 pool threads, and dns.lookup, used by fetch and http.request by default, waits for one. Measured on Node 24: with the pool busy, fetch to localhost waited for the hashes while fetch to 127.0.0.1 returned at once. The main thread is not blocked, since async hashing runs on the pool.

q: A nightly import runs Promise.all over 1,000 fs.promises.readFile calls with default settings. What really happens?
options: The OS reads all 1,000 files in parallel through its asynchronous file API
At most 4 reads run at once on the thread pool; the rest wait in its queue
They run one after another on the main thread
Node starts 1,000 threads, one per read
explain: File system calls use the libuv pool, 4 threads by default, so 996 requests queue behind the first four. That queue also delays dns.lookup and async crypto for the rest of the process, which is why you bound the concurrency yourself (for example 10 to 20 files at a time) instead of firing everything.

q: A webhook endpoint calls JSON.parse on 150 MB bodies and blocks the loop for about 2 seconds each time. Which fix actually helps?
options: Split the parse into chunks with await setImmediate() between them
Defer the parse with process.nextTick
Limit the body size, and parse large payloads off the main thread or with a streaming parser
Move the parse into an async function
explain: JSON.parse is one indivisible synchronous call, so you cannot chunk it from outside, and nextTick or async only delay it on the same thread. A size limit protects the loop, and a streaming parser or a worker handles legitimately large payloads. Also ask why one webhook sends 150 MB.

q: Whenever a customer downloads a large CSV export, the whole API slows down for several seconds. Exports take about 4 seconds of CPU and must not be lost if a pod restarts. Which design would you ship?
options: Enqueue an export job, answer 202 Accepted, and let a worker service write the file to object storage
Run the export in a Piscina worker inside the API process and stream the result
Add replicas until the slowdown is no longer noticed
Make the export function async and add await between rows
explain: Seconds of work that must survive a restart is the case for a queue and a separate worker service. A Piscina worker would unblock the loop, but the job dies with the pod and competes for the API pod's CPU. Replicas only spread the pain, and awaiting between rows with microtasks does not yield to the loop.

q: What happens when this code runs?
options: The worker dies silently and the main thread prints "main still alive"
The main thread receives the error as a normal message
Node restarts the worker automatically
The error is emitted as an 'error' event on the Worker; with no listener, the whole process exits with code 1
explain: An uncaught error ends the worker and is emitted as 'error' on the Worker object, and an 'error' event with no listener throws. Measured on Node 24: the process exited with code 1 before the timer fired. A worker pool must listen for 'error', reject the job and replace the worker; Piscina does this for you.

q: Profiling shows each request uses about 25 ms of main-thread CPU. The product team expects 600 requests per second at peak. What is the minimum number of single-process replicas, before headroom?
options: 4, because each replica handles many concurrent connections
1, if UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is raised to 64
explain: One main thread gives at most 1000 / 25 = 40 requests per second, so 600 requests per second need at least 600 / 40 = 15 replicas, before headroom. Open connections are cheap but CPU time is not, and the thread pool never runs your request handlers.

q: On an idle service, monitorEventLoopDelay() with default options reports a minimum of about 10.5 ms (after dividing by 1e6). What does that tell you?
options: The loop is blocked about 10 ms on every turn
The value includes the 10 ms sampling interval, so the real delay is about 0.5 ms
The histogram is in microseconds, so the delay is about 10 µs
The garbage collector pauses the process every 10 ms
explain: Each sample is the full gap between two ticks of a timer that fires every resolution milliseconds (10 by default); Node's source records that gap with RecordDelta. So subtract the resolution: about 0.5 ms of real delay. The values are in nanoseconds, not microseconds.

q: At peak, the dashboards show event loop utilization at 0.97, event loop delay p99 at 450 ms, every route slow at once, and PostgreSQL latency flat. What do you do first?
options: Add read replicas to PostgreSQL
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 32
Record a CPU profile to find the hot function on the main thread
Increase the HTTP server keep-alive timeout
explain: ELU near 1 with high delay, all routes slow and a flat database is the signature of CPU-bound JavaScript on the main thread. A CPU profile (node --cpu-prof, or the inspector on a canary) names the function to fix. The database is not the bottleneck, and the thread pool does not run JavaScript.

q: In code review you find this handler. What is the problem?
options: It keeps serving from an unknown state; it should log at fatal level and exit so the orchestrator restarts the process
It should also catch unhandled rejections, then keep serving
logger.error is too slow; console.error would be fine
It must be registered inside every request handler to work
explain: Node's documentation says it is not safe to resume normal operation after uncaughtException: connections, locks or half-written state may be broken. Log (pino's fatal flushes synchronously), exit with code 1, and let Kubernetes restart the pod. Adding a rejection handler that also continues makes the same mistake twice.

q: A data import script is started with node --permission --allow-fs-read=./data import.ts on Node 24. Which statement is true?
options: It can read ./data but also cannot open network connections
It is a sandbox: even malicious dependencies cannot escape it
It can read ./data, cannot read other folders or spawn processes, and can still call fetch
The flag is experimental in Node 24 and ignored in production
explain: The permission model restricts the file system, child processes, worker threads, addons and WASI; in Node 24 it does not restrict network access (a fetch succeeded in our test). The documentation calls it a "seat belt" for trusted code, not protection against malicious code. It is stable since 23.5 and 22.13.

q: A developer starts a service with PORT=9000 node --env-file=.env server.ts, and .env contains PORT=3000. What is process.env.PORT?
options: "3000", because the file is loaded last
"9000", because a variable already set in the environment takes precedence
Node exits with an error because the variable is defined twice
"3000,9000", because Node concatenates both values
explain: The Node documentation states that when a variable is defined in both the environment and the file, the environment wins, and a run on Node 24 printed 9000. That is the right behaviour for containers: real environment configuration overrides the local file.

q: A colleague proposes running PM2 in cluster mode with 8 processes inside each Kubernetes pod "to use all the cores". What is the strongest objection?
options: PM2 cannot run TypeScript files
The cluster module does not work on Linux
Processes in a cluster cannot share the listening port
It hides crashes and per-process resource use from Kubernetes, which already restarts and scales single-process pods
explain: Kubernetes restarts, load-balances and scales containers, and it can only do that well when it sees each process. A process manager inside the pod restarts crashes on its own, blurs metrics and makes resource limits harder to set. Sharing the port is exactly what cluster does, so that option is false.

q: PDF generation in pure JavaScript takes 800 ms of CPU per document and slows every other request. A teammate suggests raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 16. What do you answer?
options: Good idea: 16 threads will render 16 PDFs in parallel
It will not help: the thread pool runs native operations, not your JavaScript; use a worker pool such as Piscina or a job queue
It will help only if we also mark the generator async
It will help, but only on machines with at least 16 cores
explain: The libuv pool runs fs, dns.lookup, async crypto and zlib, never your JavaScript, so the 800 ms still run on the main thread. A worker pool moves the work to threads with their own event loops; a queue moves it out of the request. Making the function async keeps it on the main thread.

q: To show a total, checkout needs the cart, the stock check and the delivery quote. Without any one of them it cannot build a valid answer. Which combinator fits?
options: Promise.allSettled, then inspect each status
Promise.all, so the first failure fails the request
Promise.any, so the fastest service answers
Promise.race, so a slow service cannot block the request
explain: Every result is required, so failing fast is the right semantics, and that is what Promise.all does. allSettled would work but waits for every call even after one has already made the answer impossible, and you would rebuild fail-fast by hand.

q: What happens to the delivery quote call here?
options: Promise.all cancels it when checkStock rejects
It is paused until someone awaits it again
It keeps running to the end; Promise.all rejects after about 30 ms
It never started, because Promise.all starts its inputs
explain: The promises were already running before Promise.all saw them, and a combinator cannot cancel anything. Measured on Node 24: the rejection arrived after about 37 ms and the slow call still finished at about 172 ms. Stopping it requires passing an AbortSignal to the HTTP call.

q: The email job sends 100 emails with at most 10 in flight. One call in ten takes 500 ms, the others 20 ms. Why is a pool faster than Promise.all on slices of 10?
options: A pool starts the next call as soon as any slot frees, while a batch waits for its slowest call before starting the next batch
A pool runs more than 10 calls at once when the calls are fast
A pool reuses the same promise for several calls
A pool sorts the calls so that the slow ones run first
explain: With batches, every slow call holds nine idle slots until it finishes. Measured: batches took 5,122 ms and a pool 1,107 ms for this workload. A pool never exceeds its limit; it only refills free slots immediately.

q: You pass { concurrency: 20, signal } to pMap but do not pass the signal to the mapper. The signal aborts while 20 emails are being sent. What happens to those 20 calls?
options: p-map aborts them through its own controller
They are dropped from memory immediately
p-map waits for them before rejecting
They keep running; p-map only rejects and stops starting new items
explain: The p-map docs say already-started mappers are not cancelled; the signal option controls the map, not your calls. To stop the HTTP calls, pass the same signal into each mapper call. The same is true when stopOnError rejects the map.

q: The payment client calls fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(50) }) and the provider needs 300 ms. What do you catch?
options: A TypeError with the message fetch failed
A DOMException named TimeoutError
A DOMException named AbortError
Nothing: the response arrives after 300 ms
explain: Measured on Node 24: a DOMException named TimeoutError. A manual controller.abort() without a reason gives AbortError, so error.name tells a deadline from a cancellation. TypeError: fetch failed is what a network failure looks like.

q: The Orders API aborts a POST to the payment provider after the request was sent. What does the abort guarantee?
options: The provider rolls back whatever it started
The provider never processes the request
Your side stops waiting and reading; the provider may still complete the operation
The request is automatically retried later
explain: Aborting closes your side of the connection. Measured with a local server: after the client aborted, the server handler still ran to the end. That is why writes need idempotency keys and a timed-out write is an unknown outcome, not a failure.

q: A downstream service answers 503. Which call is safe to retry automatically?
options: GET /orders/42
POST /payments without an idempotency key
POST /emails/send
POST /counters/visits/increment
explain: A GET is idempotent: repeating it changes nothing. Each POST may have been processed before the error came back, so a retry could charge, send or count twice. They become safe to retry only with an idempotency key that the server deduplicates.

q: Why add full jitter to exponential backoff?
options: It makes each retry faster on average than a fixed delay
It compensates for the imprecision of setTimeout
It lets a client get past a rate limit by looking random
It spreads out the retries of clients that failed at the same moment
explain: Without jitter, every client that failed in the same second retries in the same second, again and again, and the recovering service receives synchronized waves. Full jitter picks a random delay between zero and the backoff value. It does not help with rate limits; respecting Retry-After does.

q: An async generator yields shipped orders from pages 1 to 5 and releases its connection in a finally block. The consumer does break while reading page 2. What happens?
options: All 5 pages are fetched, then finally runs
Only 2 pages are fetched and finally runs
Only 2 pages are fetched and finally never runs
The break throws, because the generator is still running
explain: A generator only runs when the consumer asks for the next value, so page 3 is never requested. break calls the generator's return(), which runs finally (and disposes an await using resource the same way). Measured: two fetches, then the cleanup.

q: What does the last line print?
options: [1, 2, 3]
[1]
[]
It depends on how fast save is
explain: forEach calls the async callback and ignores the promise it returns, so the log runs before any save finishes. Measured: [], then [1, 2, 3] a moment later. Even a very fast save resolves after the current synchronous code, so the answer does not depend on timing.

q: A function declares await using first = … then await using second = …, and throws. What happens on Node 24.11?
options: Nothing is disposed, because the function threw
Both are disposed, first then second
Only second is disposed
Both are disposed, second then first
explain: Resources declared with using are disposed when the block exits, whether it returns or throws, in reverse order of declaration. Measured: "release 2" then "release 1", on success and on failure. That is the same guarantee as nested try/finally, without the nesting.

q: Two checkout requests run requestContext.run({ requestId }, handler) at the same time and interleave at every await. What does getStore() return inside each handler after an await?
options: The context of the request that called run most recently
Its own request's context
undefined, because the context is lost at the first await
The context of whichever request resumed first
explain: AsyncLocalStorage follows the asynchronous call chain, not a global variable, so each continuation sees the context of the run that started it. Verified: the request that finished second still logged its own id. Outside any run, getStore() returns undefined.

q: The first input rejects after 5 ms, the second resolves with 'ok' after 10 ms. What do Promise.race and Promise.any give?
options: Both resolve with 'ok'
race resolves with 'ok', any rejects
race rejects with boom, any resolves with 'ok'
Both reject with boom
explain: race follows whatever settles first, a rejection included. any ignores rejections until an input fulfils, and rejects with an AggregateError only if all of them reject. Both verified on Node 24.

q: Checkout computes await Promise.race(partners.map(getQuote)) to take the first delivery quote. One day a feature flag empties partners. What happens?
options: The await never settles and the request hangs
It resolves with undefined
It rejects with an AggregateError
It throws a TypeError synchronously
explain: Promise.race([]) never settles (verified: still pending after 20 ms, and it never will be). By contrast Promise.all([]) resolves to [] and Promise.any([]) rejects with an AggregateError. Guard empty inputs explicitly.

q: The nightly job must send 10,000 confirmation emails. The email provider allows 20 concurrent requests and sometimes answers 503. Which design would you ship?
options: Promise.all over all orders, with a global 30-minute timeout
Promise.all on slices of 20, retrying the whole slice when one call fails
A for loop with await, one call at a time, so the provider is never overloaded
p-map with concurrency: 20, a per-call timeout and jittered retries on 503, failures collected and reported
explain: A pool of 20 matches the provider's limit, per-call deadlines and jittered retries handle the transient 503s, and collecting failures keeps one bad address from failing 10,000 emails. Sequential calls are safe but 20 times slower than necessary, and retrying a whole slice repeats calls that already succeeded.

q: What is the bug in this limiter?
options: A task that rejects never releases its slot, so after concurrency failures nothing new ever starts
The waiting queue is LIFO, so tasks run in reverse order
It allows one more task than concurrency to run
It runs tasks sequentially, ignoring concurrency
explain: If task() rejects, the lines after the await never run, so active stays incremented and nobody is woken. Verified: with a limit of 2 and two failing tasks, the next tasks stayed pending forever. Release the slot in finally.

q: The Orders API uses a pg pool of 10 connections. A handler runs Promise.all over 500 product ids, each doing one query. What happens?
options: node-postgres opens 500 connections for the duration of the call
The 500 queries run in one database round trip
Ten queries run at a time and the rest wait in the pool's queue, holding the request and delaying every other handler that needs a connection
The pool rejects the extra 490 queries immediately
explain: The pool caps connections at its max (10 by default per the node-postgres docs) and queues the rest. One request now monopolises the pool, and other requests wait behind it. Bound the fan-out below the pool size, or replace it with one query using WHERE id = ANY($1) (M07).

q: Checkout must stop when the customer leaves or after 10 seconds, whichever comes first. What do you pass down to every function?
options: Two separate signals, and every function checks both
AbortSignal.any([clientGone.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)])
A Promise.race between the work and a 10-second timer
A shared cancelled flag checked in a setInterval
explain: AbortSignal.any returns one signal that aborts with the reason of the first input that aborts. Verified: when the user aborted first, the combined signal carried the user's reason; when the deadline passed first, it carried a TimeoutError. Every function keeps a single signal parameter.

q: A handler does Promise.race([fetch(url), rejectAfter(2000)]) and the timer wins. What happens to the HTTP request?
options: It is aborted automatically because nobody awaits it
It is queued and retried by undici
Node logs a warning and drops the socket
It keeps running: the socket stays open and the response is downloaded for nobody
explain: A race only chooses which result you see. Measured: after the timer won, the request still reached the server and its body was read later. Under load these orphans pile up. fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }) really closes the request.

q: In a plain node:http checkout handler, which code aborts the downstream work only when the client disconnects before the response is complete?
options: request.on('end', () => controller.abort())
response.on('finish', () => controller.abort())
response.on('close', () => { if (!response.writableEnded) { controller.abort(); } })
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 30_000)
explain: close fires in both cases, after a normal response and after a disconnect; writableEnded tells them apart. Verified with a local server: the client left after 120 ms and the job stopped after its second step. finish fires only after a complete response, and end belongs to the request body stream, not to the client leaving.

q: The API gateway, the Orders API and its HTTP client each make up to 4 attempts (1 + 3 retries) on failure. The payment provider is down. How many calls can one customer request send to it?
explain: Retries multiply: each of the 4 gateway attempts triggers 4 Orders API attempts, each triggering 4 client attempts, so 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. That is why the SRE book recommends retrying at one layer only, and returning a "do not retry" signal upward.

q: Your team adopts a retry budget of 10% per client, as in Google's SRE book. What does it change during a widespread outage?
options: Each request gets at most 10% of its timeout for retries
Retries stop once they exceed 10% of the client's requests, so extra load stays near 1.1× instead of nearly 3×
Only 10% of requests are allowed to fail before an alert fires
Retries are delayed by 10% more after each attempt
explain: The budget is a ratio of retries to requests per client: past 10%, failures go back to the caller without retrying. The SRE book combines it with at most 3 attempts per request and says it reduces the growth to about 1.1×. A per-request limit alone still allows nearly 3× the load when everything fails.

q: With cockatiel, the payments policy is wrap(retry(…, { maxAttempts: 3 }), circuitBreaker(…), timeout(2_000, TimeoutStrategy.Aggressive)). What does the 2-second timeout apply to?
options: To each attempt, because the first policy in wrap is the outermost
To the three attempts together
Only to the first attempt
To the time the circuit stays open
explain: The cockatiel docs define wrap(a, b, c) as a.execute(() => b.execute(() => c.execute(fn))), so the timeout is innermost and restarts for every attempt. To bound the whole operation, put a timeout outside the retry as well, or pass a deadline signal to execute.

q: A review finds this policy around createPayment, a POST to the payment provider. Which fix would you ship?
options: Keep it, and raise maxAttempts so a payment is never lost
Send an idempotency key derived from the order with every attempt, and retry only transient errors
Remove the retry and ask the user to click again on failure
Replace it with Promise.any over five parallel calls
explain: Retrying every error retries 4xx responses that will fail again, and retrying a non-idempotent POST after a timeout may charge twice. A stable idempotency key makes the provider deduplicate attempts, and classifying errors keeps retries for transient failures. Asking the user to click again has the same double-charge risk.

q: How long does this take, measured on Node 24?
options: About 150 ms or more, because each mapping call is awaited before the next one starts
About 50 ms, because the three calls run in parallel
About 0 ms, because Array.fromAsync does not await the mapper
It throws, because the input is not an async iterable
explain: Array.fromAsync awaits each mapped value in turn. Measured: 182 ms. It accepts plain arrays as well as async iterables. For parallel work with a bound, use p-map instead.

q: In an ES module on Node 24, loadOrders resolves after 100 ms and loadInvoices rejects after 10 ms. What happens?
options: It prints "caught …" after 100 ms
The rejection is silently ignored
It prints "caught …" after 10 ms
The process exits with code 1 before the try runs
explain: While the code waits on orders, invoices rejects with no handler attached yet. Node treats it as an unhandled rejection and exits with code 1; measured, nothing was printed. await Promise.all([loadOrders(), loadInvoices()]) attaches handlers to both and the same code is caught normally.

q: fetchDiscount rejects because the loyalty service is down. What does getDiscount return?
options: A promise that resolves with NO_DISCOUNT
A promise that resolves with undefined
A promise that rejects with the error from fetchDiscount
It throws synchronously
explain: Without await, the pending promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs; verified on Node 24. return await fetchDiscount(customerId) waits inside the try, and the fallback works.

q: Checkout calls auditLog.write(event) without awaiting it, to keep the response fast. A colleague proposes void auditLog.write(event) to satisfy no-floating-promises. What do you answer?
options: Fine: void handles the rejection
Better to await it, since fire-and-forget is never acceptable
Disable the rule for this file, since audit writes rarely fail
void silences the rule but a rejection still crashes the process; attach a .catch that logs it
explain: The rule's docs warn that voiding a promise does not handle it or change runtime behaviour, and an unhandled rejection exits the process. A .catch that logs keeps the response fast and makes failures visible. Fire-and-forget is acceptable when its failure is handled and the work is not critical.

q: The orders repository catches connect ECONNREFUSED and must rethrow an error that says which order failed, without losing the original. Which line?
options: throw new Error('Could not load order ' + orderId + ': ' + String(error))
throw new Error('Could not load order ' + orderId, { cause: error })
throw Object.assign(error, { message: 'Could not load order ' + orderId })
throw new AggregateError([error], 'Could not load order ' + orderId)
explain: cause keeps the original error object, with its stack and code, and Node prints it under a [cause] line (verified). Concatenating the message loses the stack and the error code. AggregateError is meant for several independent failures, not one wrapped error.

q: A TypeScript 7 project has "lib": ["es2025"] and "types": []. A developer adds await using lease = await leaseClient(pool). What happens?
options: It compiles and runs, since using is part of ES2025
Compilation fails: AsyncDisposable and Symbol.asyncDispose are missing until you add the esnext.disposable lib or @types/node
It compiles, but Node 24 throws a SyntaxError at runtime
TypeScript 7 does not support await using at all
explain: Verified with TypeScript 7.0.2, and identically with 6.0.3: with es2025 alone, the compiler reports that it cannot find AsyncDisposable and Symbol.asyncDispose; adding esnext.disposable (or esnext, or Node's types) fixes it. Node 24.11 runs the syntax natively, so there is no runtime problem.

q: Which of these Orders API endpoints gains the most from streaming its response?
options: GET /orders?page=3, which returns 50 orders as JSON
POST /webhooks/payments, which validates a 2 KB JSON body with Zod
GET /exports/orders.csv, which exports every order of the shop, millions of rows
GET /me, which returns the current user's profile
explain: The export is the only payload whose size grows with the data and has no upper bound, so buffering it can exhaust memory. The other three are small and bounded by design; streaming them adds code and makes errors harder to report for no gain.

q: In a stream created in object mode, what is a chunk?
options: Any JavaScript value, such as one database row, and highWaterMark counts these values
A Buffer of at most 16 KiB
A string already decoded as UTF-8
One line of JSON text ending with a newline
explain: Object mode lets each chunk be any value, which is what you want between your own steps (rows, events). highWaterMark then counts objects, 16 by default (measured), whatever their size. Buffers are the chunks of byte streams, not object-mode streams.

q: A scheduled export writes its gzipped CSV to a local file with await pipeline(rows, toCsvLines, createGzip(), createWriteStream(path)). The file write fails with "disk full". What happens?
options: The promise rejects, but the source stays open so you can retry the write
Every stream in the chain is destroyed, the source's cleanup runs, and the promise rejects once with the "disk full" error
Only the destination emits 'error'; the promise resolves when the source ends
pipeline retries the failed write until the disk has space
explain: Measured: with a destination failing on its third write, pipeline rejected with that error and the source generator's finally ran. Leaving the source open is what .pipe() does, which is why it leaks file handles and cursors.

q: You find source.pipe(destination) in the old export code. What does .pipe() not do?
options: It does not apply backpressure between the two streams
It does not work with object-mode streams
It does not forward any data until the source has ended
It does not destroy the other stream or report the error when one side fails
explain: .pipe() does respect backpressure and forwards chunks as they come. What it lacks is failure handling: measured, a failing source left the destination open, and a failing destination left the source paused but not destroyed. pipeline fixes both.

q: writable.write(chunk) returns false. What does it mean?
options: The chunk was dropped and must be written again
The stream is closed and will reject further writes
The buffer has reached its highWaterMark: the chunk is queued, and you should stop writing until 'drain'
An error happened and an 'error' event will follow
explain: The chunk is accepted and buffered; false is a request to pause. Measured with a mark of 10 bytes: writes of 5, 5 and 1 bytes returned true, false, false, and 'drain' fired once the buffer was empty. Nothing is dropped, which is exactly why ignoring the signal fills memory.

q: On Node 24.11, what is the default highWaterMark of fs.createReadStream(path)?
options: 16 KiB
64 KiB
1 MiB
16 objects
explain: Measured: readableHighWaterMark is 65,536 for file read streams. The general default for byte streams (including fs.createWriteStream) is 16 KiB, and 16 objects is the object-mode default, which is why 16 KiB is the tempting wrong answer.

q: What are 'é'.length and Buffer.byteLength('é')?
options: 2 and 1
1 and 1
2 and 2
1 and 2
explain: String length counts UTF-16 code units, and é is one; UTF-8 encodes it in two bytes (measured). So a Content-Length header or an upload limit computed with .length is wrong as soon as the text is not ASCII.

q: Which way of turning the catalogue's UTF-8 byte stream into text is safe when a character is split across two chunks?
options: chunk.toString('utf8') on each chunk
new TextDecoder().decode(chunk) on each chunk
One TextDecoder called with { stream: true } on each chunk, then decode() once at the end
chunk.toString('latin1') on each chunk, then re-encoding the result
explain: With { stream: true } the decoder keeps the incomplete bytes until the next chunk, and the final decode() flushes them. Measured: a decoder without that option produced caf��, the same garbage as toString(), because each call starts from scratch.

q: In Node 24, the catalogue job calls fetch(url). What is response.body?
options: A Web ReadableStream: iterate it with for await, or convert it with Readable.fromWeb to use Node stream APIs
A Node Readable that you can .pipe() directly into a file
A Buffer holding the whole response
A string decoded with the charset from the headers
explain: Measured: response.body instanceof ReadableStream is true and it is not a Node Readable, so it has no .pipe(). Readable.fromWeb(response.body) gave a Node stream of Buffer chunks that pipeline wrote to disk.

q: What does client.query(new QueryStream(sql, params, { batchSize: 500 })) from pg-query-stream give you?
options: A Readable in object mode backed by a server-side cursor: rows arrive 500 at a time as the consumer reads
A promise that resolves with every row once the query has finished
A byte stream of CSV produced by PostgreSQL's COPY command
An iterator that runs one LIMIT 500 OFFSET n query per batch
explain: The library wraps a cursor in an object-mode Readable whose highWaterMark is the batch size (100 by default, from its source). Measured: it streamed 200,000 rows in order, and destroying it closed the cursor. It is one query, not a series of OFFSET queries, so it reads one consistent snapshot.

q: How must the customer name Martin "Max" Dupont, Jr. be written in the CSV export?
options: Martin "Max" Dupont, Jr.
"Martin ""Max"" Dupont, Jr."
"Martin \"Max\" Dupont, Jr."
Martin ""Max"" Dupont\, Jr.
explain: RFC 4180 wraps a field that contains a comma, a quote or a line break in double quotes, and doubles each quote inside; the csvField function produced exactly that (measured). CSV has no backslash escaping, so the backslash options produce broken columns.

q: With its defaults, what does new Upload({ client, params: { Bucket, Key, Body: stream } }).done() do with a 22 MiB catalogue stream?
options: It reads the whole stream into memory, then sends one PutObject
It starts a multipart upload, sends 5 MiB parts with up to 4 in flight, then completes the upload
It sends 22 parts of 1 MiB, one after the other
It writes the stream to a temporary file, then uploads the file
explain: Measured against a fake S3: CreateMultipartUpload, parts of 5, 5, 5, 5 and 2 MiB, then CompleteMultipartUpload. partSize defaults to 5 MiB (the S3 minimum) and queueSize to 4, so memory stays around 20 MiB per upload. Only a body smaller than one part became a single PutObject.

q: A teammate proposes to stream the request body of POST /webhooks/payments (a 3 KB JSON object validated with Zod) "for performance". What is your answer in the review?
options: Agree: streaming is always faster than reading the whole body
Disagree: the body is small and bounded by a body limit, and it must be complete to be validated, so reading it whole is simpler and correct
Agree, provided the body is read as a Web stream instead of a Node stream
Disagree, because streams are deprecated in recent Node versions
explain: Streams pay off when the size grows with the data; a 3 KB payment webhook is bounded and needs to be complete before validation anyway. Streaming it would add code and error paths for no memory gain. Streams are not deprecated; they are just the wrong tool here.

q: What does this code print?
options: undefined, because pipeline resolves with nothing
It throws, because the last step of a pipeline must be a Writable
3
['a', 'b', 'c']
explain: When the last step is an async function, pipeline resolves with what it returns; measured, it printed 3 (three one-character chunks). It is a clean way to write "consume and summarise" steps without a Writable class.

q: An older catalogue import copies a local file to an upload stream like this. The upload stream fails halfway. What happens to file?
options: It is destroyed with the same error and its file descriptor is closed
It keeps reading the whole file into memory
It stays open and paused: nothing destroys it, so its file descriptor stays open
Its 'error' event fires with the upload error
explain: Measured: after the destination failed, the .pipe() source was paused (readableFlowing false) and not destroyed. Under load that leaks file descriptors. await pipeline(file, uploadStream) destroys both and gives you one error to handle.

q: A scheduled export for the finance team must give up after 10 minutes and release its cursor and file handle. Which implementation would you ship?
options: await pipeline(rows, toCsvLines, createGzip(), createWriteStream(path), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(600_000) })
setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 600_000) next to the pipeline
Promise.race([pipeline(…), sleep(600_000)])
Calling destination.end() from a timer after 10 minutes
explain: Aborting the signal destroys every stream in the chain; measured, the promise rejected with AbortError and the source generator's finally ran. Promise.race only stops waiting: the streams keep running and holding their resources. Exiting the process skips all cleanup.

q: The Orders API lets the accounting firm download monthly invoice archives of up to 2 GB, often over slow connections. What happens with this route?
options: The file is read at the speed of the client
res.write throws once the client falls behind
Chunks are dropped when the client cannot keep up
The return value of write is ignored, so unsent data piles up in the response buffer, up to the whole file
explain: Measured with a 31 MiB source and a slow destination: the destination buffered 31.3 MiB, the entire input, against 16 KiB with pipeline. Nothing is dropped and nothing throws, which is what makes the bug invisible until memory runs out. Fix: await pipeline(file, res).

q: Which call to write is the first to return false?
options: The 1st, because 1 MB is already above 16 KiB
The 16th, because in object mode the mark counts objects (16 by default), so about 16 MB is buffered by then
None: object-mode streams have no backpressure
The 17th, because the mark is only exceeded after 16 objects
explain: Measured: the call at index 15, the 16th, returned false. In object mode highWaterMark counts objects whatever their size, so large rows can hold far more memory than the number suggests; lower the mark or batch smaller.

q: A fraud job scans for await (const row of Readable.from(readOrders())) and breaks at the first suspicious order. readOrders is an async generator that closes a cursor in its finally. What happens on break?
options: The stream is destroyed and the generator's finally runs, so the cursor is closed
The generator keeps running in the background until the query ends
The stream is paused and the cursor stays open until garbage collection
An ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE error is thrown out of the loop
explain: Measured: after break, stream.destroyed was true and the generator's finally had run. Leaving a for await loop early calls return() on the iterator, which destroys the stream; no error is thrown to the caller.

q: The catalogue import does text += chunk.toString() for every chunk of a UTF-8 file. Suppliers with accented product names report garbled characters, but only on some lines. What is the cause?
options: The files are not really UTF-8
toString() defaults to Latin-1
A multi-byte character is sometimes split across two chunks, and each half is decoded on its own
Chunks are delivered out of order under load
explain: Measured: café cut between the two bytes of é decoded to caf��. It only happens when a chunk boundary falls inside a character, hence "only some lines". toString() defaults to UTF-8; the fix is a stateful decoder (setEncoding, TextDecoder with stream: true, readline).

q: A Hono version of the export streams from a generator that yields strings. What happens when the body is read?
options: It works: Response encodes strings to UTF-8 automatically
It works, but every line arrives as a separate HTTP response
Hono rejects the route at startup because the body is not a Node stream
Reading fails with TypeError: Received non-Uint8Array chunk, because a Response body must carry bytes
explain: Measured: reading a Response built on string chunks failed with exactly that TypeError. Encode on the way: ReadableStream.from(csvLines()).pipeThrough(new TextEncoderStream()), or yield Buffers. Only a string passed as the whole body is encoded for you.

q: The team writes a shared library that streams the full product price list. It is used by the Orders API (Fastify) and by the back-office dashboard's Next.js route handler. Which stream type should its public API return?
options: A Node Readable, because the Orders API is the bigger consumer
A full array of rows, because streams do not cross framework boundaries
An EventEmitter that emits one event per row
A Web ReadableStream, which the route handler returns as is and the Fastify service converts with Readable.fromWeb
explain: Web Streams are the standard that Fetch-style frameworks expect, and Node converts them in one call at the edge of the Fastify service. Returning a Node Readable would force the Next.js side to convert instead and tie the library to Node APIs; an array defeats the purpose of streaming.

q: The orders export runs its pipeline with rows from pg-query-stream, and releases the client in finally. Someone in finance closes the tab halfway. What happens?
options: pipeline rejects with ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE, destroys the query stream (closing the cursor), and finally releases the connection
The query keeps reading every row until the end, then the client is released
The response buffers the remaining rows in memory until the process restarts
Node crashes with an unhandled stream error
explain: Measured against PostgreSQL over the wire protocol: the server logged ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE, the generator's cleanup ran, the connection was released, and the next query on the same pooled connection succeeded. That is exactly why the export goes through pipeline.

q: A CSV export has sent 3 million lines when the database connection drops. What should the finance team experience?
options: A 500 status with a JSON error body
A failed download: the response is destroyed, so the client sees a broken transfer instead of a file that looks complete
A normal end of file, so finance keeps the rows already exported
The error message written as the last line of the CSV
explain: The 200 status and headers are already sent and cannot change. pipeline destroys the response; measured, a fetch client got 200 and then response.text() rejected with TypeError: terminated. Ending normally would deliver a silently truncated file, which is worse than a visible failure.

q: This export code follows an old README. After a few dozen cancelled downloads, every request on the service hangs. Why?
options: pipeline does not work with pg-query-stream, so the query never starts
Cancelled downloads leave a lock on the orders table
A destroyed stream emits 'close' but never 'end', so cancelled exports never release their connection and the pool runs dry
The 'end' listener releases the client twice, which corrupts the pool
explain: Measured: a Readable destroyed before its end emitted 'close' only. Each cancelled download therefore keeps its pooled connection, and once the pool is exhausted every pool.connect() waits. Release in a finally around the pipeline, which runs on success, error and disconnect alike.

q: A customer registers with the name =HYPERLINK("https://evil.example","Invoice"). Your finance team opens the orders export in a spreadsheet. What should csvField do?
options: Nothing: RFC 4180 quoting already makes the cell safe
Reject the export with a 400 error
Strip every = character from all fields
Prefix text cells that start with =, +, -, @, a tab or a line break with a single quote, so the spreadsheet shows them as text
explain: Quoting only protects the CSV structure; the spreadsheet still evaluates a cell that starts with =. OWASP recommends the single-quote prefix, and it applies to text only so that -3 stays a number (measured: =SUM(A1:A9) became '=SUM(A1:A9), -3 stayed -3).

q: This Fastify route limits catalogue files to 20 MiB. A supplier uploads a 25 MiB file. What happens?
options: Fastify answers 413 before the upload starts
The route answers 201 and stores a 20 MiB truncated object; only part.file.truncated says so
request.file() throws RequestFileTooLargeError and nothing is uploaded
upload.done() rejects and the multipart upload is aborted
explain: Measured with @fastify/multipart 10.1.6: 201, a 20 MiB object completed in the bucket, and truncated set to true, with no error. When you stream the file yourself, the library's README tells you to listen to 'limit' or check truncated; destroying the stream on 'limit' made upload.done() reject and abort the multipart upload (measured).

q: The supplier portal, a browser app, will let suppliers upload product videos of up to 2 GB. The backend only needs to know where each video is stored. Which design do you propose?
options: The API returns a presigned PUT URL; the browser uploads straight to S3, and the API records the key afterwards
The API streams the multipart body into Upload from @aws-sdk/lib-storage
The API reads each video with toBuffer() and sends one PutObject
The browser sends base64 chunks in JSON requests that the API reassembles
explain: When the server does nothing with the bytes, they should not pass through it: no memory, bandwidth or request timeout spent on 2 GB bodies. Streaming into Upload is the right choice only when the server must scan, transform or encrypt the content, or the client cannot talk to S3. Buffering and base64 multiply memory use.

q: Finance wants a "download every order since 2019" button. A test run takes 25 minutes. What do you build?
options: A background job that streams the rows into S3 with Upload, then notifies the user with a presigned GET link that expires
A streamed HTTP response, with the load balancer's idle timeout raised to one hour
An endpoint that builds the file in memory, then sends it with Content-Length
A streamed response that the client resumes with Range headers when it breaks
explain: Twenty-five minutes on the request path must survive proxy timeouts, rolling deploys and the user's network, and holds a database connection all along. A job can retry and run on its own workers, and the link outlives a closed tab. A streamed CSV generated on the fly cannot be resumed with Range, since there is no stored file to address.

q: A pod with a 512 MiB memory limit is OOM-killed during a catalogue upload peak, yet the dashboards show heapUsed steady at 80 MiB. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The heap limit is too low: raise --max-old-space-size to 1024
A memory leak in the JavaScript heap that the dashboards sample too slowly to see
Buffers live outside the JavaScript heap: concurrent uploads each hold up to queueSize × partSize of part buffers, which only the RSS shows
Kubernetes counts the size of the files on disk towards the pod's memory
explain: Measured: 200 MiB of Buffers left heapUsed unchanged and added 200 MiB to arrayBuffers and the RSS, which is what the container limit enforces. With the default 4 × 5 MiB per upload, 25 concurrent uploads already need about 500 MiB. Raising the heap limit does nothing for Buffers; cap concurrency or part buffering, or use presigned uploads.

q: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess on, what is the type of first?
code:
declare const orders: Order[];
const first = orders[0];
options: Order
Order | null
Order | undefined
Readonly<Order> | undefined
explain: The array may be empty, so reading an index can give undefined; measured, assigning it to a non-optional variable fails with TS2322. Without the flag the type is Order, which is the lie the flag exists to remove. Nothing in JavaScript returns null for a missing index.

q: types.ts exports an interface Order and a constant x. Without verbatimModuleSyntax, main.ts does import { Order, x } from './types.ts'. What happens with node main.ts on Node 24?
options: It crashes at startup: the module does not provide an export named Order
It runs, because Node sees that Order is only used as a type and drops it
It runs, and Order is undefined wherever the code reads it as a value
Node reports a type error on Order and exits before running anything
explain: Measured: SyntaxError: The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'Order'. Node only strips type syntax; an import without type is kept as a value import, and interfaces do not exist at runtime. Node never type-checks, so it cannot know Order is a type; verbatimModuleSyntax reports TS1484 at compile time instead.

q: Which of these files runs with node file.ts on Node 24, without extra flags?
options: One with enum Status { Draft, Paid } used to tag order rows
One with a class using constructor(private readonly url: string)
One with namespace Billing { export const vat = 0.2; } for tax rates
One with a union type, satisfies and a type-only declare namespace
explain: Node strips erasable syntax only. Measured: enums, parameter properties and namespaces with code all fail with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX because they generate JavaScript. Types, satisfies and a type-only declare namespace disappear entirely, so that file ran.

q: Which statement about TypeScript 7.0 is correct as of October 2026?
options: It is a preview only, published as @typescript/native-preview until 7.1 is out
It is the stable typescript package, run as tsc, with no programmatic API yet
It adds a tsgo command that replaces tsc and accepts every 6.0 option
It is a runtime that executes TypeScript and replaces Node's type stripping
explain: TypeScript 7.0 was released on 8 July 2026; npm shows typescript 7.0.2, and the announcement says it “does not ship with an API”, with a new one planned for 7.1. The native preview package was the pre-release channel. Options deprecated in 6.0 are removed in 7.0, and it is a compiler, not a runtime.

q: toResponseBody(order: PublicOrder) returns JSON.stringify(order), where PublicOrder has id, status and totalCents. It is called with a database row held in a variable, which also has paymentToken. What happens?
options: Compile error: paymentToken does not exist in PublicOrder
It compiles and the JSON contains paymentToken
It compiles and TypeScript removes paymentToken from the output
It compiles but throws at runtime
explain: Structural typing only requires the fields the type asks for, and types do not exist at runtime to remove anything; measured on Node 24, the token was in the JSON. The excess property error (TS2353) applies only to an object literal written directly at that spot, not to a variable holding a row.

q: applyOrderEvent ends its switch (event.type) with default: return assertNever(event);. A colleague adds { type: 'partial_refund'; at: Date } to OrderEvent but no case. What happens?
options: Partial refunds fall into default and throw at runtime only
Nothing visible until the first partial refund reaches the service
tsc fails at assertNever(event): partial_refund is not assignable to never
tsc fails on the OrderEvent declaration, which has an unhandled member
explain: Once the handled cases are removed, event still contains the partial_refund member, which cannot go into a never parameter: measured TS2345. The runtime throw in assertNever is only a backup; the point is that the build fails first. The union type itself is perfectly valid.

q: With the typed EventBus of the lesson, and orderId, paymentId, totalCents and amountCents variables of the right branded types, which call compiles?
options: bus.emit('order.paid', { orderId, totalCents })
bus.emit('order.payed', { orderId, paymentId })
bus.on('order.placed', async (event) => audit.log(event.paymentId))
bus.emit('order.refunded', { orderId, amountCents })
explain: The name constrains the payload through DomainEvents[E]. Measured: the first call passes a totalCents that an order.paid payload does not have (TS2353) and misses paymentId, the misspelled name is not in keyof DomainEvents (TS2345), and an order.placed payload has no paymentId (TS2339). The refunded event has exactly the required fields.

q: With OrderId and PaymentId branded as in the lesson, which line compiles?
options: const text: string = toOrderId('ord_1');
loadOrder('ord_' + order.number);
loadOrder(refund.paymentId);
const id: OrderId = 'ord_' + crypto.randomUUID();
explain: A branded value is a string plus a compile-time marker, so it can be used as a string. The other direction is blocked: measured, a plain string or a PaymentId passed as an OrderId fails with TS2345. Only the checking function, with its single as OrderId, creates one.

q: const routes = { home: '/', orders: '/orders' } satisfies Record<string, string>; What is the type of routes.orders?
options: '/orders'
string
string | undefined
Record<string, string>
explain: Measured: assigning routes.orders to a '/orders' variable fails, so the literal widened to string, because the target type asks for string. The keys stay known, so there is no undefined, unlike an annotation with noUncheckedIndexedAccess. as const satisfies would keep '/orders'.

q: A client posts { customerId: 'cus_1', items: [...], isAdmin: true } to POST /orders, which uses PlaceOrderBody.safeParse(req.body), built with z.object and no isAdmin field. What is in parsed.data?
options: Every field, isAdmin included
Nothing: success is false because of the unknown key
Every field except isAdmin
isAdmin set to undefined
explain: Measured with Zod 4.6.7: success was true and isAdmin was absent, because z.object strips unknown keys. That protects against mass assignment. Rejecting the request is what z.strictObject does (issue code unrecognized_keys).

q: The Orders API calls the payment provider through a client generated with openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch. What do the generated types guarantee at runtime?
options: That responses match the spec, because openapi-fetch validates each body against it
That the provider cannot change its contract without breaking your build first
That 4xx and 5xx responses are thrown as typed exceptions you can catch
Nothing at runtime: responses are typed from the spec but never checked
explain: Generated types are compile-time only; the docs describe data and error typed from the spec, not validated. If the provider sends something else, your code receives it. For an API you do not control, parse the response with a schema. openapi-fetch returns errors in error; it does not throw them.

q: With strict on, what does tsc say about catch (error) { console.log(error.message); }?
options: 'error' is of type 'unknown' (TS18046)
Nothing: error is typed Error
Nothing: error is typed any
That catch needs an explicit type annotation
explain: strict includes useUnknownInCatchVariables, because JavaScript can throw any value, a string included. Measured: TS18046. Narrow first with error instanceof Error. It was any before that flag, which is what older code still assumes.

q: This helper merges the options of the delivery partner's HTTP client. What does it print, and which flag would have refused the call?
options: { timeoutMs: 5000, retries: 2 }; no flag needed, the spread skips undefined values
{ timeoutMs: undefined, retries: 2 }; strictNullChecks
{ timeoutMs: undefined, retries: 2 }; exactOptionalPropertyTypes
{ timeoutMs: 5000, retries: 2 }; noUncheckedIndexedAccess
explain: Measured: a key present with the value undefined overwrites the default in a spread, so the client ends up with no timeout. exactOptionalPropertyTypes makes timeoutMs?: number mean “absent or a number” and rejects the call (TS2379). strictNullChecks alone accepts it, because an optional property normally allows undefined.

q: A team wants to drop the build step of its NestJS service and run node src/main.ts in production on Node 24. Their tsconfig has erasableSyntaxOnly and tsc passes. What do you tell them?
options: It works: erasableSyntaxOnly guarantees Node can strip the code
It fails on the decorators, which tsc accepts under that flag; keep a tsc or SWC build
It works once they add a reflect-metadata import at the top of main.ts
It works, but startup is slower because Node type-checks first
explain: Measured: a decorated class compiled cleanly under erasableSyntaxOnly, then failed in Node with SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token. NestJS also needs emitDecoratorMetadata for dependency injection, which only a real compiler (tsc, or SWC through the Nest CLI) produces. Node never type-checks.

q: In a pnpm monorepo, @acme/contracts exports ./index.ts and the Orders API runs it unbuilt with Node 24 type stripping. It works locally. After the package is published to the private registry and installed in another repo, startup fails. Why?
options: Node will not strip types under node_modules; the workspace link pointed outside it
The registry removes .ts files from published packages unless files lists them
pnpm compiles workspace packages on install, and a registry install skips that step
The consuming repo lacks rewriteRelativeImportExtensions in its tsconfig
explain: Measured: a linked workspace package ran because Node follows the link to the real path, while a .ts file inside node_modules failed with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING. A published package must ship compiled JavaScript. tsconfig flags do not matter to Node, which ignores tsconfig.

q: A service uses tsx watch locally and an esbuild bundle in production. A pull request that passes null to a function expecting a string was merged and crashed in production. Which fix do you ship?
options: Replace esbuild with tsdown, which type-checks every file while it bundles
Switch the dev loop from tsx to node --watch src/main.ts, which checks types
Add a CI step running tsc --noEmit that blocks the merge on errors
Turn on strict in tsconfig so that esbuild rejects type errors
explain: tsx documents that it does not type-check (measured: const s: string = 42 ran), and esbuild and tsdown transform code without checking it; Node's type stripping does not check either. Only tsc (6.0 or 7.0) checks types, so it must run in CI. tsconfig flags change what tsc reports, not what a bundler does.

q: Your backend monorepo wants TypeScript 7's speed in CI, but it uses type-aware lint rules that call the TypeScript API. What is the plan the TypeScript team recommends?
options: Wait for 7.1, because 7.0 cannot type-check a project that also runs a type-aware linter
Install 7.0 everywhere and turn the type-aware lint rules off until they are rewritten
Stay on 6.0 only, because 7.0 dropped module: nodenext along with node10
Use 7.0 for tsc and keep 6.0 beside it via @typescript/typescript6 for lint
explain: The 7.0 announcement says it ships no API yet and describes installing @typescript/typescript6 (command tsc6) next to 7.0 for tools that need the 6.0 API. Waiting is not required: the type check itself works on 7.0. nodenext is supported; it is node10 resolution that was removed.

q: What is the risk in this webhook code?
options: The predicate checks one key but claims a full RefundEvent, and the compiler trusts it
It does not compile: the in operator cannot be used on a value typed unknown
value is RefundEvent makes TypeScript insert a runtime check of every field
None: after typeof value === 'object' the compiler has proven the shape
explain: A type predicate is a promise the compiler does not verify: once it returns true, body is a full RefundEvent everywhere. Any object with a type key passes, so refund(undefined, undefined) can run. Use a schema (RefundEvent.safeParse) for anything beyond one field. The in check does compile after the object and null checks.

q: Using the lesson's applyOrderEvent, what happens with applyOrderEvent(pendingOrder, { type: 'refund', at: new Date() }), where pendingOrder has status: 'pending_payment'?
options: It returns a refunded order with refundedAt set to the event date
It returns the pending order unchanged and logs nothing
It throws InvalidTransitionError: only paid orders can be refunded
It does not compile: a pending order cannot be passed with a refund event
explain: The refund case only returns when order.status === 'paid'; otherwise it breaks out of the switch and reaches the throw. Measured on Node 24: “Cannot refund an order that is pending_payment”. The parameter types allow any pair of order and event, so this rule is checked at runtime, in one place.

q: A reviewer proposes replacing default: return assertNever(event); with default: return order; “to be safe”. What do you answer?
options: Agreed: returning the order unchanged avoids crashes in production
Refuse: a new event type would then compile and be silently ignored
It makes no difference: tsc checks exhaustiveness on every switch anyway
Agreed, as long as noFallthroughCasesInSwitch is enabled in the tsconfig
explain: With a value-returning default, event is never required to be never: measured, adding a partial_refund event then compiled without an error, and those events would be dropped without a trace. tsc does not check exhaustiveness by itself: the never assignment is what creates the check. noFallthroughCasesInSwitch is about cases without break, not about missing ones.

q: With Express 5 and @types/express, what does tsc report for this route?
options: Nothing: req.params is a Record<string, string> for every route
Both properties are string | undefined under noUncheckedIndexedAccess
An error on orderId, because route params must be validated before use
TS2339 on customerId: the route string is parsed into the params type
explain: The Express types use template literal types to read :orderId out of the route string, so req.params is { orderId: string }. Measured with @types/express 5.0.6: TS2339 on customerId only. A plain dictionary type would be the case if the route were a variable of type string.

q: What is AggregateOf<'order.placed' | 'payment.captured'>?
code:
type AggregateOf<Name extends string> =
  Name extends `${infer Aggregate}.${string}` ? Aggregate : never;
options: never, because a union does not extend the pattern
'order' | 'payment'
string
'order.placed' | 'payment.captured'
explain: A conditional type on a naked type parameter is distributive: it runs once per union member and joins the results. Measured: 'order' and 'payment' are accepted and 'placed' is rejected (TS2322). never would be the result for a name without a dot.

q: A checkout converts a price string with Number(price) * 100 before saving integer cents. For '19.99', what does Node 24 compute, and what do you change?
options: 1999; nothing to change, doubles are exact up to two decimal places
1999, because V8 rounds every multiplication result to 15 significant digits
1998.9999999999998; convert the decimal string to exact integer cents at the edge
1998.9999999999998; store it in a double precision column instead of an integer
explain: Measured: 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998, because 19.99 has no exact binary representation. Truncating it gives 1998 cents, a lost cent per item. Convert once, at the edge, to an exact integer, then compute in integer cents; floating-point columns only move the problem.

q: A developer wants enum OrderStatus { PendingPayment = 'pending_payment', Paid = 'paid' } in the Orders API, which runs under Node 24 type stripping with erasableSyntaxOnly. What do you propose?
options: A const enum, because tsc inlines its values and erases the declaration
Keep the enum and start production with --experimental-transform-types
A namespace OrderStatus holding one exported constant per status
An as const object plus a union type derived from its values
explain: The as const object gives runtime values, readable strings in JSON and logs, and a union type through (typeof OrderStatus)[keyof typeof OrderStatus], all erasable. Measured: a const enum is rejected too, with TS1294 under the flag and ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX in Node. Namespaces with code fail the same way, and the transform flag printed an ExperimentalWarning on Node 24.11 and no longer exists in Node 26.

q: Why write const retryPolicies = { … } satisfies Record<string, RetryPolicy> rather than const retryPolicies: Record<string, RetryPolicy> = { … }?
options: Only satisfies keeps the known keys, so retryPolicies.paymentProvider is never undefined
Only satisfies catches backoff: 'fixd'; the annotation accepts any string there
satisfies also freezes the object at runtime, like Object.freeze
satisfies makes every nested property readonly, like as const
explain: Both forms check the value against the type (measured TS2820 on 'fixd' with satisfies). The difference is the variable's type: the annotation turns it into a Record, so under noUncheckedIndexedAccess every lookup is possibly undefined (TS18048); satisfies keeps the inferred shape. It is a type-level operator: nothing happens at runtime.

q: The env schema has PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000), with no .min. A deploy sets PORT= (empty). What value does the service get?
options: 3000, because an empty string counts as missing
A validation error: an empty string is not a number
0, because Number('') is 0
NaN, rejected by .int()
explain: Measured with Zod 4.6.7: z.coerce.number() turned '' into 0. The default only applies to undefined, not to an empty string, and Number('') is 0, not NaN. Listening on port 0 lets the OS pick a random port, so the service starts and nobody can reach it; add .min(1).

q: Your service validates tRPC 11 procedure inputs with Zod. An edge function team wants Valibot 1.5 for its smaller bundles. What changes on the tRPC side?
options: Nothing specific: Valibot implements Standard Schema, which tRPC accepts
tRPC needs a Valibot adapter package, the same way it needed one for Zod
Valibot schemas must first be converted to Zod with a code generation step in CI
tRPC only accepts Zod schemas, so the edge team has to keep Zod
explain: Standard Schema is a shared interface: a ~standard property with version, vendor and validate. Zod 4.6.7, Valibot 1.5.0 and ArkType 2.2.9 implement it (measured), and the tRPC docs list Standard Schema among accepted validators. Adapters were needed before this interface existed.

q: The Orders API is called by your own React back office, a partner's Java service and an Android app in Kotlin. Which way of sharing types fits?
options: tRPC, because it removes the need to write any schema
An OpenAPI document, with a generated client per language
A shared npm package of TypeScript types that every client installs
A hand-written description of each endpoint, kept in a wiki
explain: OpenAPI is language-neutral, so every client can generate code from the same contract, and the document doubles as public documentation. tRPC's types travel through TypeScript imports, which a Java or Kotlin client cannot use. A shared TypeScript package has the same problem, and a wiki drifts from the code.

q: With strict on, why does this compile?
options: strict types every rejection reason as Error, so the read is checked
tsc infers the type of error from the errors chargeCard can throw
error is unknown, and reading nested properties on an unknown value is allowed
Its parameter is typed any: the strict catch rule covers only catch clauses
explain: The flag only covers catch clauses. The lib types a rejection reason as any, so measured, error.whatever.deep compiled inside .catch, and a network error without response would crash the handler. Prefer await inside try/catch, or annotate (error: unknown). TypeScript has no checked exceptions to infer from.

q: chargeCard can fail because the card is declined or because the payment provider times out. Which design would you approve?
options: Throw a typed exception for both and list them in a TSDoc @throws comment
Return the declined card as a value; throw on the timeout with a cause
Return null for both failures and log the reason at warning level
Return a Result for both, and for every database and network failure too
explain: A declined card is an expected outcome the caller must handle (tell the customer), so it belongs in the return type. A timeout is an incident: throwing it with cause lets retries, the error middleware and alerting deal with it. TypeScript cannot type thrown exceptions, so a comment is not enforced; returning Result for every infrastructure failure clutters every call site.

q: According to RFC 9110, which methods are idempotent?
options: GET and POST, because both are the most common methods
Only the safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE
PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE)
Every method except PATCH, which RFC 5789 excludes
explain: RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." The tempting answer "every method except PATCH" forgets POST, which is neither safe nor idempotent; that is why POST /orders needs an idempotency key to be retried.

q: An order resource has status, shippingAddress and note. The app sends PUT /orders/ord_42 with only { "note": "leave at door" }. What does that request mean?
options: Replace the whole order with this body, so the omitted fields are reset or removed
Change the note and keep the other fields, exactly like a PATCH
Nothing: PUT can only create resources, so the server must answer 405
Append the note to the order history, because PUT is not idempotent
explain: PUT sends the complete new state of the resource at that URL; what you omit is not kept. Treating it like PATCH is the tempting misreading: to change one field, send PATCH with a JSON Merge Patch body (RFC 7396). PUT is idempotent, and it can create or replace.

q: A customer with a valid access token calls DELETE /products/prd_3, a route reserved for back-office staff. Which status fits?
options: 401 Unauthorized, with a WWW-Authenticate header
403 Forbidden: the caller is known but not allowed
400 Bad Request, because the request should not have been sent
409 Conflict, because the role conflicts with the operation
