To free the memory used by the old data before writing the new value
explain: A refetch started before the click carries the old server state; if it resolves after setQueryData, the toggle jumps back. Cancelling it removes that window. setQueryData does not throw during a fetch, which is exactly why the race exists.

q: A teammate says: "We do not need TanStack Query, we load the orders once in a Context provider." Which argument is the strongest?
options: Context can only hold primitive values and stable functions, not arrays of objects
Context does not cache, dedupe, expire or invalidate: we would rebuild that
Context is deprecated in React 19 in favour of the use hook and stores
Context values cannot be read from custom hooks, only from components
explain: Context only hands a value down the tree; every concern of server state (freshness, sharing requests, invalidation after writes, cancellation) would be hand-written. It is fine for rarely-changing client values. React 19 did not deprecate Context; it added the <Context value> provider syntax.

q: This back office component re-renders on every keystroke in an unrelated search box (the search text is in Redux). Why?
options: The search reducer mutates the selection slice by accident on each keystroke
useSelector re-renders the component after every action, whatever it returns
Destructuring the result subscribes the component to the whole store
The selector builds a new object on each call, and the check is ===
explain: useSelector re-runs after every dispatched action but re-renders only when the result is a new reference, and an object literal always is. Select each value separately, pass shallowEqual, or memoise. The second option is the tempting half-truth: the selector re-runs every time, the render does not have to.

q: A Zustand cart store is read by a badge with useCartStore((state) => state.lines.length). An "add to wishlist" action in the same store changes only state.wishlist. Does the badge re-render?
options: No: the selected length is unchanged, and Zustand compares it with ===
Yes: every set call re-renders every component subscribed to the store
Yes, unless the store is created inside a provider at the root of the app
No, because Zustand only re-renders components on route navigation
explain: Zustand's README says it detects changes with strict equality on the selected value. A primitive like a length stays equal, so no re-render. A selector building a new object would re-render each time; useShallow is the fix there. Zustand needs no provider.

q: Why does the button never show "Placing your order…"?
options: useFormStatus only works with Server Functions, not with client actions
It only reads a form rendered by a parent: move the button into a child
The action must first be wrapped in startTransition to report its status
The button needs a formAction prop instead of type="submit" to be tracked
explain: Measured: pending stayed false in the component that renders the form and became true in a child. The docs state the hook only reports on a parent form. It works with any function action, not only Server Functions.

q: A checkout form uses useActionState and does not disable its button. The customer double-clicks. What happens?
options: React ignores the second submit while the first one is still pending
The second submit aborts the first request and only the second order is sent
Both run, one after the other: React queues them, so two orders are posted
Both run in parallel, and the server keeps whichever request finishes first
explain: Measured: two clicks, two action calls, the second starting when the first finished (the docs: calls are queued and run sequentially). Nothing is aborted or ignored. Disable the button with useFormStatus and send the same idempotency key so the server answers a duplicate with the first order.

q: The checkout action catches a 503 and returns { error }. The customer sees the error, and the email field is now empty. Why?
options: React resets uncontrolled fields after the action, even with an error state
The 503 response told the browser to clear its autofill data for the whole form
useActionState remounts the form with fresh fields on every new state
The email input lost its name attribute when the error was rendered
explain: The docs say uncontrolled fields are reset after the action succeeds, and an action that returns normally has succeeded. Measured: the field was empty after a returned error, and kept the email with defaultValue={state.email}. The form is not remounted; the fields are reset to their default values.

q: After a successful save, the notes list briefly shows the new note twice: once saved, once "sending". What is the fix?
options: Call addOptimisticNote after the await, once the server has answered
Wrap the setNotes that follows the await in startTransition
Give the optimistic note the same key as the saved note so React merges them
Replace useOptimistic with useState and remove the note manually on success
explain: Updates after an await are not yet part of the Action (react.dev documents this caveat), so setNotes rendered while the optimistic note was still applied. Measured: a duplicate frame without startTransition, none with it. Moving the optimistic call after the await would remove the instant feedback.

q: The refund form converts euros to cents with values.amountEuros * 100. An agent enters 19.99. What does the API receive?
options: 1999, because multiplying by 100 shifts the decimal point exactly
1998, because JavaScript truncates the fraction when it multiplies
1998.9999999999998: round with Math.round before sending
19.99, because a number input sends its value as typed
explain: Measured in Node: 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998, because 19.99 has no exact binary representation. Truncation would give 1998, one cent short. Math.round(19.99 * 100) gives 1999.

q: An agent filters the orders table on shipped while on page 4 (a cursor in the URL). The new list shows rows that do not match, or an error. What is the bug?
options: The query key does not include the filters, so the old page is served
The old cursor was kept, but it belongs to the previous filtered list
The status should live in useState, which updates faster than the URL can
React Router caches the previous search params for the current route
explain: A keyset cursor (M05) encodes a position in one list; reused with another filter it points to nothing meaningful, and the API may reject it. The hook in section 2 deletes the cursor whenever the filter changes. A missing filter in the key would show stale rows, not mismatched pages.

q: The cart lives in useState in the product page component, which renders the header, the filter panel and 20 cards directly. One item is added. What re-renders?
options: Only the header, because it is the only component that shows the count
The header and the card that was clicked, because they took part in the event
Nothing until the cart is saved to the server and the response arrives
The page and everything it renders, cards and filter panel included
explain: A state change re-renders its component and, by default, every child it renders. Measured: 20 cards and the filter panel re-rendered. Moving the cart into a provider that receives the page as children, with actions split out, reduced it to the badge.

q: "My orders" uses useInfiniteQuery and the customer has loaded 5 pages. After cancelling an order, the code invalidates the query. What happens?
options: Only the first page is refetched, and the other four pages are dropped
All 5 pages are refetched in sequence, each cursor from the previous page
All 5 pages are refetched in parallel, one request per stored cursor
Nothing happens: infinite queries are never matched by invalidateQueries calls
explain: Measured with two loaded pages: the refetch requested page 1, then page 2, in sequence, since the second cursor comes from the first response. With many pages that is a slow chain; maxPages limits how many pages are kept.

q: A teammate proposes a Zustand store with orders and a loadOrders() action, called on app start, "so every screen has the orders". Which answer would you give in review?
options: No: orders are server state; use TanStack Query and its shared cache
Yes, but with Redux Toolkit instead, because it is the standard for global state
Yes, as long as the store is persisted to localStorage between visits
No: put the orders in a Context provider so that they load only once
explain: A client store would hold a second copy of server data, with no staleness, deduplication or invalidation: the stale-status bug again. Redux Toolkit or Context change the container, not the problem. If the codebase is already on Redux, RTK Query is the equivalent of TanStack Query there.

q: What is the main difference between a Server Component and a Client Component rendered with SSR?
options: A Server Component produces HTML on the server, while SSR produces a JSON payload that the browser turns into HTML
Its code never reaches the browser; an SSR-rendered Client Component still ships its code to hydrate
SSR runs only once at build time, while Server Components run on every request and cannot be cached
Server Components cannot fetch data themselves, so SSR is still needed for every page that shows data
explain: SSR is about when HTML is produced; a Client Component rendered that way still sends its JavaScript so it can hydrate. A Server Component runs only on the server, at build or request time, and sends none. The first option inverts things: the RSC Payload is the serialised output of Server Components, and HTML comes from prerendering.

q: add-to-cart-button.tsx starts with 'use client' and imports formatPrice from lib/money.ts, which has no directive. Where does formatPrice end up?
options: Only on the server, because a module without a directive defaults to the server
It depends on whether formatPrice is async: async helpers always stay on the server
Nowhere: the build fails until lib/money.ts gets its own 'use client'
In the client bundle, because the directive covers everything the module imports
explain: React documents that 'use client' marks the module and its transitive dependencies as client code, so you do not repeat the directive in every helper. Having no directive does not keep a module on the server; only import 'server-only' would turn that import into a build error.

q: Which prop can the product page (a Server Component) pass to a Client Component?
options: A promise of the reviews, which the Client Component unwraps with use() inside a Suspense boundary
An onAddToCart arrow function defined in the page, which the button calls on click
A Product class instance, so the button can call product.formatPrice() itself
A Symbol('cart') created in the page, used as a stable identity for the cart
explain: Promises are in React's list of serialisable props, and Next.js documents passing an unawaited promise and reading it with use() under Suspense. Plain functions (other than Server Functions), class instances and symbols not registered with Symbol.for cannot cross the boundary.

q: The header and the price box both call getCurrentCustomer, wrapped with React.cache in a shared module. What does that guarantee?
options: The customer is cached across requests for as long as the session cookie is valid
The result is shared between all visitors until the next deploy invalidates it
Within one server request, components calling the same wrapped function share one call
The result is memoized in the browser too, so hydration does not fetch the customer again
explain: React clears the cache for each server request and shares it only among components that call the same memoized function during rendering. It is not a cross-request cache (that is 'use cache'), so the first two options are wrong, and it is for Server Components, not the browser.

q: A page renders a heading and a price inside <Suspense fallback="Loading price...">; the price resolves after 300 ms. What does renderToReadableStream send?
options: Nothing until the price resolves, then the whole page in a single chunk
The heading and the fallback first, then the price with a small swap script
The price first, because suspended content is sent with a higher priority than the shell
The complete page twice: once with the fallback and once more with the price
explain: Measured on React 19.3.1: the first chunk left at 58 ms with the heading and "Loading price...", the second at 305 ms with the price in a hidden element and the inline swap script. Waiting for everything is what non-streaming rendering would need; renderToString does not even wait and sends the fallback.

q: The server rendered "Delivered by Tuesday" and the first client render produces "Delivered by Wednesday". What did React 19.3.1 do (measured)?
options: It reported a recoverable error and rebuilt the tree on the client: Wednesday
It kept Tuesday silently: hydration ignores text differences
It threw an uncaught error, and the customer saw a blank page instead of the product
It patched only the text node to Wednesday, without reporting anything to monitoring
explain: Measured with hydrateRoot in jsdom: onRecoverableError received "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client", and the DOM ended with the client text. Keeping the server text happens only with suppressHydrationWarning.

q: With Cache Components enabled, a component reads cookies() and is not inside any Suspense boundary. What happens?
options: cookies() returns an empty cookie store during prerendering, without any warning
The whole application silently switches to request-time rendering, page by page
Next.js caches it per visitor, keyed on the cookie
Next.js flags the route as blocking and asks you to add a Suspense boundary
explain: Cache Components requires runtime data to sit behind a Suspense boundary so every route keeps a static shell; the dev overlay shows the blocking-route insight and the build guides you to fix it. Returning empty values is what dynamic = 'force-static' does in the previous model, not this one.

q: In a Server Action, a customer updates their saved delivery address, and the page must show the new address in the same response. Which call?
options: revalidateTag('address-' + customer.id, 'max')
revalidatePath('/') from a Client Component
updateTag('address-' + customer.id)
cacheLife('seconds') on the address reader
explain: updateTag expires the tag immediately, for read-your-own-writes, and is reserved for Server Actions. revalidateTag with a profile is stale-while-revalidate: the action's own re-render does not wait for fresh data, so the customer could still see the old address.

q: Which statement about a Server Action exported from app/checkout/actions.ts is true?
options: Anyone able to send the POST can call it, so it must check the session, ownership and input itself
It is private, because Next.js encrypts action ids and removes the actions you do not use
The sign-in check in app/checkout/page.tsx protects it too, since the page renders the form
Only the form that imports it can call it, because Next.js compares Origin and Host
explain: Next.js documents that actions are reachable by direct POST requests and that a page-level check does not extend to the actions it renders. Encrypted ids and dead-code removal reduce exposure but are explicitly not a substitute for checks inside each action; the Origin check stops cross-site forms, not a direct request.

q: Where should ORDERS_API_CLIENT_SECRET live in the storefront?
options: NEXT_PUBLIC_ORDERS_API_CLIENT_SECRET, so Client Components can call the API directly
An unprefixed variable, read only in a DAL module that imports server-only
publicRuntimeConfig in next.config.ts, which keeps it out of the JavaScript bundle
localStorage, written by the login page and sent by the browser on each call
explain: Unprefixed variables stay on the server, and server-only turns an accidental import from a Client Component into a build error. A NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable is inlined into the browser bundle, which publishes the secret; publicRuntimeConfig was removed in Next.js 16.

q: app/products/[slug]/error.tsx exists. Which error does it not catch?
options: An error thrown while rendering page.tsx in the same folder
An error thrown by a nested layout in a subfolder
An error thrown while rendering a Client Component used by the page
An error thrown by app/products/[slug]/layout.tsx
explain: Next.js documents that error.js wraps the page, loading, not-found and nested layouts, but not the layout.js of its own segment. An error there goes to the parent's boundary, or to global-error.tsx for the root layout.

q: An old product page uses getStaticPaths with fallback: 'blocking'. What replaces it in the App Router?
options: An async Server Component without caching, the equivalent of getServerSideProps
A Route Handler in route.ts that returns the list of paths to the build
generateStaticParams, plus dynamicParams for unlisted slugs
A loading.tsx shown during generation
explain: The migration guide maps getStaticPaths to generateStaticParams and the fallback option to dynamicParams; 'blocking' has no direct equivalent because streaming made the difference negligible. Route Handlers replace pages/api, not static paths.

q: An interviewer asks: "Is 'use server' the opposite of 'use client'?" Which answer is accurate?
options: No: Server Components have no directive; 'use server' marks Server Functions
Yes: 'use server' marks a component as a Server Component, the default being client
Yes, but only in Next.js
No: 'use server' marks code that runs once at build time and never per request
explain: react.dev says it directly: a common misunderstanding is that Server Components are denoted by 'use server', but there is no directive for them; the directive is for Server Functions. That is also why a file marked 'use server' exposes callable endpoints.

q: Each call takes about 200 ms and none depends on another. Which change would you ship?
options: Wrap the three functions with React.cache so their results are reused within the request
Mark the page 'use client' so the browser fetches the three in parallel after hydration
Promise.all for product and stock; reviews in a child under Suspense
Add a loading.tsx and keep the code
explain: The three sequential awaits are a server waterfall of about 600 ms; parallel requests cut it to the slowest one, and streaming the optional reviews keeps the LCP content from waiting. React.cache only deduplicates repeated calls, and loading.tsx shows a fallback but leaves the waterfall in place.

q: How many times does fetchCurrentCustomer run in one request?
options: Once: cache recognises that both wrappers point to the same underlying function
Twice: each call to cache creates a new memoized function with its own, separate cache
Zero: cache defers the call until a Client Component actually reads the customer
Once per customer, because the memoized value is shared across their requests
explain: React documents that calling cache with the same function several times returns different memoized functions that do not share a cache, so components must import one memoized function defined at module level. And the cache never spans requests, which rules out the last option.

q: The page renders its header, then a component inside <Suspense> fetches the product and calls notFound() because it does not exist. What does the crawler receive?
options: A 404 status with the not-found UI, since notFound() sets it
A 500 status, because notFound() throws while the response streams
A 410 status, because Next.js knows the product was deleted
A 200 status with the not-found UI and a noindex meta tag
explain: Streaming responses start with 200 and the first chunk fixes the status; Next.js then streams the not-found UI and adds noindex so the URL leaves the index. To return a real 404, check existence in the page before the first Suspense boundary.

q: A returning customer has 3 items in a cart stored in localStorage. What happens on page load?
options: A mismatch: the server renders 0 and the client 3; read storage after mount
It works: the typeof window check is the recommended way to avoid hydration errors
The server throws a ReferenceError on localStorage and the whole page fails to render
React patches 0 into 3 silently
explain: The check runs differently on the server and in the browser, so the first client render differs from the HTML: measured in jsdom, the server sent 0, hydration reported a text mismatch and the badge ended at 3 after a client re-render. The guard avoids the ReferenceError, which is why the code looks safe, but it creates the mismatch.

q: A CMS description renders as <p><p>In stock</p></p> in a Client Component. React renders the same elements on server and client. Why does hydration still fail?
options: React's reconciler refuses nested paragraphs on the client, but accepts them on the server
Next.js minification drops the inner paragraph
The browser's parser closes the first <p> at the second, so the DOM differs
The server escapes the inner paragraph as text, so the client sees different content
explain: Measured in Chromium 156: the markup became <p></p><p>In stock</p><p></p>, so React found a different DOM and reported a hydration error, after warning that a <p> cannot be a descendant of a <p>. The fix is valid markup, such as a <div> wrapper.

q: After the December 2025 advisory (CVE-2025-55182), a colleague says the storefront is safe because it defines no Server Functions. Your answer?
options: Agreed: only apps that expose Server Function endpoints were affected by that advisory
Not necessarily: apps supporting RSC could be vulnerable without them; patch
Agreed: hosting providers blocked the exploit at their edge, so no upgrade is needed
Only the Pages Router parts are affected, so finishing the App Router migration fixes it
explain: The React post states that an app may still be vulnerable if it supports React Server Components even without Server Function endpoints, and that hosting mitigations must not replace an immediate update. Apps without a server or without an RSC-capable framework were not affected.

q: What is wrong with this cached function?
options: Nothing: Next.js adds the cookie value to the cache key automatically for cached functions
The lifetime is too long for a price
getCurrentCustomer must also be wrapped with React.cache for the key to work
Cached functions cannot read cookies, even via a helper: pass the id in
explain: Next.js documents that 'use cache' scopes cannot access cookies() or headers(), and the restriction follows the call stack, failing with next-request-in-use-cache. Passing the customer id as an argument makes it part of the key; nothing is added to the key automatically.

q: The back office calls the storefront's POST /api/revalidate Route Handler after an agent edits a description. A few seconds of stale content are fine, and the handler must not block. Which call?
options: updateTag('product-' + slug) from the handler
revalidatePath('/', 'layout') to clear everything
revalidateTag('product-' + slug, 'max')
cacheLife('seconds') on getProduct instead
explain: revalidateTag with a profile gives stale-while-revalidate and is allowed in Route Handlers; tags invalidate just that product. updateTag is restricted to Server Actions, invalidating the root layout path is far wider than needed, and a seconds lifetime takes the product out of the static shell for every visitor.

q: A candidate says: "fetch in a Server Component is cached by default." Which answer is accurate as of October 2026?
options: True in Next.js 14; not by default since Next.js 15; with Cache Components you cache explicitly with 'use cache'
True in every version: Next.js always caches GET requests made with fetch until a revalidation
False in every version: Next.js has never cached fetch results, only whole rendered pages
True only when Cache Components is enabled, because it caches every fetch made during render
explain: Next.js 15 changed the default: fetch requests and GET Route Handlers are no longer cached by default, and Cache Components (Next.js 16) makes caching opt-in with directives. Cache Components does the opposite of the last option. Stating the version first is the point of the question.

q: What is the vulnerability in this Server Action?
options: It lacks a CSRF token, and Next.js does not check the origin of Server Action requests
No ownership check: any signed-in customer can cancel any order by its id
It should be a GET Route Handler, because cancelling an order twice is idempotent anyway
Throwing on a missing session leaks the stack trace and the message to the customer
explain: Authentication is checked, authorisation of the object is not: the order id comes from the client, so this is an IDOR. Next.js already compares Origin and Host for actions, and production errors from the server reach the browser as a generic message with a digest, so the other options are not the issue.

q: A double click created two orders. A teammate says: "Next.js dispatches Server Actions one at a time per client, so this cannot happen any more." Your answer?
options: Correct: sequential dispatch makes every Server Action idempotent on the server side
Disabling the button while the action is pending is enough; no server change is needed
Call it through Promise.all to merge clicks
Dispatch is client-side; the server does not queue: use an idempotency key
explain: The Next.js docs state that sequential dispatch belongs to the client dispatcher and that the server runs each action as it arrives: a second tab, a retry or a replayed POST still creates a second request. Only a key stored by the Orders API (M05) makes the retry return the first order.

q: An attacker adds totalCents=1 to the form data of the "Place order" form. What does parsed.data contain (measured with Zod 4.6.7)?
code:
const PlaceOrderInput = z.object({ cartId: z.uuid(), idempotencyKey: z.uuid() });
const parsed = PlaceOrderInput.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
options: Only cartId and idempotencyKey: keys the schema does not declare are dropped
cartId, idempotencyKey and totalCents: '1', kept as a string
Nothing: safeParse fails because the object contains an unknown key
totalCents: 1, converted to a number, next to the two ids
explain: A Zod object strips keys it does not declare: the measured result held only the two UUIDs. Failing on unknown keys would need a strict object. And the action never reads a price from the client anyway: the Orders API computes the total.

q: The order is created, yet the customer sees "Could not place the order." Why?
options: redirect is forbidden in Server Actions
createOrder throws after the order is saved, because the API answers 201 Created
redirect throws, and the catch swallows it: call it after the try/catch
redirect needs an explicit 303 status argument when it is called in a Server Action
explain: The redirect docs say it throws a control-flow error and must be called outside the try block; here the catch turns a successful redirect into an error message. Redirects are allowed in Server Actions, and Next.js picks 303 itself for form submissions without JavaScript.

q: The back office (a separate Vite app) must notify the storefront after a product edit. Server Action or Route Handler?
options: A Server Action, since both are POST requests and the action id is in the client bundle
A Route Handler: a stable URL for callers other than your own UI
A proxy.ts rule that intercepts the call and invalidates the product before routing
A Client Component calling router.refresh()
explain: Server Actions are referenced by build-specific encrypted ids, meant to be called by your own React UI; another app needs a stable endpoint. A Route Handler exposes POST /api/revalidate, checks a shared secret and calls revalidateTag. A proxy rule only intercepts requests before routing.

q: CI builds one image with NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYMENT_ENV=sandbox; production runs the same image with NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYMENT_ENV=live. What does browser code read?
options: live, because the runtime environment variable always wins
An empty string, because the build and runtime values conflict
Nothing: the container refuses to start when a public value changes
sandbox, because public variables are inlined at build time
explain: Next.js documents that NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the JavaScript during next build and frozen: a single image promoted across environments keeps the build value. Per-environment values must be read on the server at request time. Replacement by an empty string is what happens to unprefixed variables in client code.

q: In production, the Orders API fails while a Server Component renders, and error.tsx displays error.message. What does the customer see?
options: The original message with the full stack trace from the server
A generic message, with a digest you can match against the server logs
The JSON error body that the Orders API returned to the server
An empty string, because server errors are never forwarded to it
explain: Next.js replaces the message of errors forwarded from Server Components with a generic one plus a digest, to avoid leaking sensitive details; the original message reaches the browser only in development. That is why error.tsx should log the error and show a fixed sentence.

q: Which of the shop's screens would you not move to Server Components?
options: The back office orders table: logged in, no SEO, heavy client state
The storefront product page, which must be indexed by Google and paint fast on mobile
The marketing landing pages, which change only when the content team publishes in the CMS
The order confirmation page, which shows one order read from the Orders API
explain: Server Components pay off for SEO, first paint and keeping data access on the server; a logged-in, highly interactive table gains little and already runs well as a Vite SPA with TanStack Query. The other three screens are exactly where a static shell and server data help most.

q: A Card must accept as children some text, a number, several elements, or nothing at all. Which type should its children prop have?
options: ReactElement
ReactNode
JSX.Element
string | ReactElement[]
explain: ReactNode is the union of everything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, booleans, null, undefined and iterables of nodes. ReactElement is the tempting answer, but it accepts only JSX elements: text fails with TS2747 and a number with TS2322.

q: What does ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> give the shop's Button?
options: Only the event handlers of a native button, such as onClick and onFocus
The props of the Button component itself, read from its definition
Every native <button> prop except ref
Every native button prop, with each one made required
explain: It is the full set of native button props (handlers, disabled, type, aria-*), so the component can intersect it with its own props and spread the rest onto the element. Only the "WithoutRef" part removes something: ref, which ComponentProps<'button'> includes (measured with @types/react 19.3.0).

q: With the React 19 types, what is the type of inputRef after const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)?
options: RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>: check current before use
MutableRefObject<HTMLInputElement>, so current is never null
RefObject<HTMLInputElement>, whose current React sets before the first render runs
Ref<HTMLInputElement>, which cannot be read directly
explain: Measured: the assignment to RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null> compiles, and inputRef.current.focus() fails with TS18047 ("possibly null"). current really is null until React attaches the element, and the types say so; inputRef.current?.focus() is the fix.

q: In React 19, how should the shared SearchField let the order search form focus its input?
options: Wrap it in forwardRef, which React 19 requires for any ref
Expose a focus() method through a context
Pass the ref under another name, such as inputRef, because ref is reserved
Declare a ref prop typed Ref<HTMLInputElement> and pass it on
explain: Since React 19, a function component receives ref as an ordinary prop, and react.dev says forwardRef is no longer necessary and will be deprecated. forwardRef still works, which makes it tempting, but new components do not need it, and renaming the prop was a workaround from before React 19.

q: Why does the team replace { isLoading: boolean; isError: boolean; error?: Error; data?: OrderSummary[] } with a union on status?
options: A union renders faster, because React compares a single status field instead of four separate flags
Each state holds only its own fields, so impossible combinations cannot be written
Booleans are not allowed in props under strict mode
The union lets the component skip the error state entirely
explain: Four independent fields allow 16 shapes, such as loading and error at once; the union allows exactly three, and inside if (state.status === 'success') the compiler knows data exists. Performance is not the reason: types are erased before React ever runs.

q: In LinkActionProps, what is the job of onClick?: never?
options: It makes the link's click handler optional
It strips onClick from the rendered <a> at runtime, so the handler never fires
It makes onClick together with href a compile error
It tells React to ignore click events on links
explain: No value has type never, so the link member accepts onClick only when it is absent; with href and onClick together, no member matches and tsc reports TS2322. Types have no effect at runtime, which rules out the second option.

q: The orders screen renders <DataTable rows={orders} getRowKey={…} columns={[…]} /> with no type argument. Where does Row come from?
options: It is inferred from rows, and the columns are checked against it
It defaults to any, because no type argument was written at the call site
It defaults to unknown, so render must narrow each row
It is read from the key of the first column
explain: TypeScript infers a component's type parameters from its props, like any function call; rows={orders} makes Row the order type. That is why { key: 'total' } fails with TS2322 once the field is totalCents. Nothing falls back to any, which is precisely what the old table did.

q: What is the main cost of the polymorphic Text with an as prop, as measured in the lesson?
options: It renders an extra wrapper around the chosen element, which breaks CSS selectors
It cannot accept children
It only works with HTML tags, not with components
Unreadable errors, an unchecked implementation, slower type-checking
explain: Inside, the element is a plain ElementType; the errors dump nested Omit types; and 200 uses added about 9,200 instantiations against 21 for a plain button (tsc 6.0.3). It renders exactly one element and accepts components such as a router Link as well as tags.

q: Why does the cart context use createContext<CartContextValue | null>(null) with a useCart hook that throws on null?
options: Because createContext requires null as its default whenever the value is an object
A missing provider fails loudly, and callers get a non-null value
Because use cannot read a context whose default is an object
It makes the context cheaper to re-render
explain: The throw turns a missing provider into an error with a clear message (measured: "useCart must be used inside <CartProvider>"), and the check removes null from the returned type. A fake default object would compile too, which is why it is tempting, but it hides the missing provider, as the empty cart did.

q: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes on, which value is a valid OrderPatch = Partial<Pick<OrderDetail, 'shippingAddress' | 'deliveryNote'>>, where deliveryNote: string | null?
options: { deliveryNote: undefined }
{ status: 'refunded' }
{ deliveryNote: null }
{ deliveryNote: 42 }
explain: null is part of the field's type, so it compiles, and the API reads it as "clear the note". undefined looks harmless, but under exactOptionalPropertyTypes an optional key means "absent", not "set to undefined", and tsc rejects it with TS2375. status is not picked (TS2353).

q: The badge map is declared { … } as const satisfies Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>. A developer adds the status cancelled to OrderStatus. What happens?
options: The map fails to compile until it has a cancelled entry
The badge for cancelled falls back to the first entry
Nothing at compile time; the badge shows undefined at runtime
The map compiles, but statusBadges.paid.icon widens to string
explain: Record<OrderStatus, …> requires one key per status, and satisfies checks the object against it: measured, a missing key fails with TS1360 in tsc 6.0.3 (TS2741 in 7.0.2). Literal types are kept by as const, so paid.icon stays 'check'.

q: In the old fetcher, const body = await response.json(); body.anything.goes; compiled. Why?
options: response.json() returns Promise<unknown>, and unknown allows property access
TypeScript skips type checking inside async functions
The fetch types infer the body type from the URL
json() returns Promise<any> in the DOM types, which turns checks off
explain: The DOM types declare json() as returning Promise<any>, and everything read from an any is any too. unknown is the opposite: reading a property on it fails until you narrow or parse, which is why the fixed fetcher writes const body: unknown.

q: What does tsc report for the last line?
options: Nothing: a string is a valid React element
TS2747: IconSlot does not accept text as a child
TS2322 on the return statement: a component cannot return its children prop directly
TS2503: ReactElement is not exported by the React 19 types
explain: Measured with @types/react 19.3.0: "'IconSlot' components don't accept text as child elements" (TS2747). A string is a valid ReactNode, not a ReactElement, which is the confusion behind the first option. Returning children is fine because a ReactElement is a valid return value.

q: After upgrading the storefront to the React 19 types, const emptyState: JSX.Element = <p>No orders yet</p>; fails with TS2503. Which fix would you ship?
options: Add "jsx": "preserve" to tsconfig.json
Type it as any until the React types are fixed upstream in DefinitelyTyped
Import JSX from react, or let TypeScript infer the type
Downgrade @types/react to the previous major version
explain: The React 19 types no longer declare a global JSX namespace, hence "Cannot find namespace 'JSX'"; importing it from react compiles (measured), and most of the time the annotation is not needed at all. The jsx option controls how JSX is emitted, not where the namespace comes from.

q: Which line fails to compile, and why?
options: The last line (TS18048): isLoading does not rule out a pending query that is not fetching
error.message: the error is typed unknown by default
The destructuring line: a discriminated union loses its narrowing as soon as it is destructured
None: after both checks, data is always defined
explain: Measured with TanStack Query 5.104.5: "'data' is possibly 'undefined'" (TS18048) on the last line. The reference defines isLoading as isFetching && isPending, so a disabled query passes both checks; early returns on isPending and isError compile, destructured or not. The default error type is Error, not unknown.

q: An interviewer asks you to type the state of a "refund order" request in the back office (not started, running, failed with a message, done with a refund id). Which design would you defend?
options: { isRunning: boolean; isDone: boolean; error?: string; refundId?: string }
A string enum RefundState plus a separate refundId variable
{ state: string; payload: any }, so new states need no type change
A union on status: idle, running, failed with message, done with refundId
explain: The union puts each field in the only state where it exists, so refundId can be read only after checking status === 'done', and adding a state is caught by the exhaustiveness check from M04. The flags look simpler but allow running and done at once, and any gives up checking.

q: A colleague types the shared action as below. What happens on the last line?
options: TS2322: the object matches neither member
It compiles: excess property checks accept a key of any member
TS2353: onClick does not exist on LinkProps
It compiles, and Action calls refundOrder when the agent clicks the rendered link
explain: Measured: no error. On a union, the excess property check accepts any key that exists in some member, so the call is assignable to LinkProps; the component then renders a link and silently drops the handler. Adding onClick?: never to LinkProps and href?: never to ClickProps turns it into TS2322.

q: This line, in status-pill.tsx, breaks the build with TS17008. What is the bug?
code: export const StatusPill = (props: { value: T; format: (value: T) => string }) => {props.format(props.value)};
options: Arrow functions cannot be generic in TypeScript
A component can only have a type parameter when it is declared with React.FC<Props>
In .tsx, <T> parses as a JSX tag: write <T,> or a function
T needs a constraint such as T extends object
explain: Measured: "JSX element 'T' has no corresponding closing tag" (TS17008), a parse error, not a type error. <T,> or a function declaration removes the ambiguity. Generic arrows are fine in .ts files, and React.FC makes generics harder, not possible.

q: The refund dialog renders <Select options={refundReasons} value="broken" onChange={trackReason} getLabel={…} />, where refundReasons is ['damaged', 'late_delivery', 'wrong_item'] as const and trackReason accepts any string. It compiles. Which change makes it fail?
options: Type value as NoInfer<Option> in SelectProps
Remove as const from refundReasons
Add Option extends string as a constraint
Type options as Option[] instead of readonly Option[]
explain: Without NoInfer, TypeScript collects candidates from value too and widens Option to include "broken"; with it, only options decides and the call fails with TS2322 (both measured). A string constraint still accepts "broken", and removing as const widens Option to string, the opposite of the goal.

q: A teammate proposes an as prop on every component of @shop/ui, buttons and dialogs included, "for flexibility". What is the senior answer?
options: Agree: once the types compile, polymorphism costs nothing to the team or to the compiler
Agree, but write the props with any to keep compile times low
Refuse all polymorphism and wrap native elements by hand in every app
Keep as for a few primitives; use separate components elsewhere
explain: The cost is real and measured: unreadable errors, an unchecked implementation, and about 9,200 instantiations for 200 uses. Primitives earn it; a button that becomes a link changes behaviour, so separate components (or Radix asChild, Base UI render) are clearer. Refusing everything is the over-correction.

q: What does tsc report on the last line?
options: Nothing: TypeScript infers the tuple [boolean, () => void] from the array literal
TS2349: the inferred type is an array, so toggleCart may be a boolean
TS2554: useDisclosure expects one argument
TS2304: toggleCart is not defined
explain: An array literal is inferred as an array of the union of its elements, not as a tuple. Measured: TS2349 ("Not all constituents … are callable"), plus TS2722 under noUncheckedIndexedAccess. return [isOpen, toggle] as const gives readonly [boolean, () => void]. The argument has a default value, so the call with none is valid.

q: Why does setOrders([order]) fail with TS2322 here, and what is the fix?
options: It is inferred as never[]; write useState<OrderSummary[]>([])
State arrays are read-only; use orders.push(order) instead
setOrders only accepts a function; write setOrders(() => [order])
The state is any[], which strict mode refuses; add as OrderSummary[] to the call
explain: With nothing to infer from, an empty array literal gives never[] under strict settings, and measured, "Type 'OrderSummary' is not assignable to type 'never'" (TS2322). A type argument states the intent. Mutating with push would compile against a typed array, but React would not re-render.

q: What does tsc report for the first export?
options: Nothing: Omit removes id from each member and keeps the other fields
TS2322: status must be 'paid' | 'refunded'
TS2353: Omit on a union keeps only shared keys
TS2741: refundedAt is missing
explain: Omit is a mapped type over keyof OrderView, and the keys of a union are those its members share: here only status (measured: the second export compiles, and paidAt fails with TS2353). A distributive version, T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never, applies Omit to each member.

q: Asked to "write a pick that keeps key safety", which signature would you ship?
options: function pick<T>(source: T, keys: string[]): Partial<T>
function pick<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(source: T, keys: readonly K[]): Pick<T, K>
function pick(source: object, keys: string[]): Record<string, unknown>
function pick<T, K extends string>(source: T, keys: K[]): Record<K, unknown>
explain: K extends keyof T rejects unknown keys (measured: 'total' fails with TS2322), and the Pick<T, K> return type knows exactly which keys exist (.totalCents fails with TS2339). Partial<T> looks close, but it accepts any string key and returns every field as optional.

q: What is the type Statuses?
options: string
never, because a readonly tuple is not an array
readonly ['paid', 'shipped']
'paid' | 'shipped'
explain: The tuple matches readonly (infer Item)[], and infer captures the element type, the union of its literal members (measured: assigning 'refunded' fails with TS2322). It would be never without readonly in the pattern, because a readonly tuple does not match a mutable array type. as const keeps the literals, so it is not string.

q: Which call fails to compile with the lesson's buildPath and RouteParams?
options: buildPath('/orders/:orderId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k' })
buildPath('/orders', {})
buildPath('/orders/:orderId/refunds/:refundId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k' })
buildPath('/orders/:orderId/refunds/:refundId', { orderId: 'ord_7f3k', refundId: 'ref_2b' })
explain: The conditional type extracts both orderId and refundId from the pattern, so an object without refundId fails (TS2345 in tsc 6.0.3, TS2741 in 7.0.2, both measured). A pattern with no parameter yields {}, so buildPath('/orders', {}) compiles.

q: The badge map must have one entry per OrderStatus, and statusBadges.paid.icon must keep the type 'check'. Which declaration does both?
options: const statusBadges = { … } as const satisfies Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>
const statusBadges: Readonly<Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>> = { … } as const
const statusBadges = { … } as Record<OrderStatus, BadgeStyle>
const statusBadges = { … } as const
explain: satisfies checks every key and value against the record without changing the variable's type, and as const keeps the literals. The annotated version also checks the keys, which makes it tempting, but the annotation, not as const, decides the variable's type: measured, paid.icon widens to the whole icon union (TS2322 against 'check'). as even accepted an object with three statuses missing, and as const alone checks nothing.

q: Which fix for Monday's NaN € incident would you ship?
options: Write useQuery<Order[]>(…) so that the data is typed at every call site of the hook
Replace as Order[] with as unknown as Order[], which is stricter
Parse the body as unknown with a schema in fetchOrders
Rename the field back to total in the BFF and add a comment
explain: Only a runtime check can catch a payload that changed after the build; measured with Zod 4.6.7, the old body fails at path ["items", 0, "totalCents"]. A type argument on useQuery is the same unchecked claim as as, moved elsewhere, and as unknown as is looser, not stricter.

q: In code review you see const order = 5 as Order; fail with TS2352, and the author "fixes" it with 5 as unknown as Order. What do you say?
options: Approve: the double cast is the documented way to convert types
Ask for a real fix: the double cast silences the only check
Approve, but ask for satisfies Order on the next line
Ask for <Order>5, the angle-bracket cast, which TypeScript checks more strictly than as
explain: as refuses only conversions with no overlap (TS2352, measured); going through unknown removes even that, and the program still holds a number where an Order is expected. Angle-bracket casts are the same assertion with another syntax, and they do not parse in .tsx files.

q: An interviewer asks: "Enum or literal union for the order statuses in the back office?" Which answer fits the lesson?
options: An enum, because only enums give named constants
An enum, because a union cannot be iterated at runtime
Either one: since TypeScript 5, both compile to the same JavaScript object at runtime
A literal union, plus an as const object when runtime values are needed
explain: Measured: a string enum fails under erasableSyntaxOnly (TS1294), and label('paid') fails with TS2345 when the parameter is the enum. An as const object gives named constants and an iterable list, which covers the two reasons people pick enums. They do not compile to the same JavaScript: a union emits nothing, an enum emits an object.

q: Which test would have caught the Pay button that stayed disabled after a declined card?
options: A snapshot of the checkout's first render, updated whenever the markup changes on purpose
A test asserting that the submitted state becomes true on click and false after a success
A component test that answers POST /orders with 402, clicks Pay, then expects Pay enabled
A unit test checking that placeOrder throws a typed error on a 402 response
explain: Only that test reaches the declined-card path and checks what the customer can do next. The snapshot records the first render, the state test checks an implementation detail (it would pass with the bug), and the unit test proves placeOrder throws but says nothing about the button.

q: Which checkout behaviour cannot be checked reliably in a jsdom component test?
options: The alert shown after a 402 response, with the text the customer reads
The order summary staying visible while the customer scrolls
The Pay button being disabled while the order request is in flight
The accessible name the address field gets from its label element
explain: jsdom has no layout engine: measured, getBoundingClientRect() returned zeros and IntersectionObserver was undefined, so scrolling and sticky positioning need a real browser. The other three are DOM state and accessibility information, which jsdom and Testing Library handle well.

q: Which query should a test use first to find the Pay button?
options: screen.getByTestId('checkout-pay-button')
container.querySelector('button.btn-primary')
screen.getByText('Pay', { selector: 'button' })
screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })
explain: Testing Library ranks getByRole first: it finds the element the way assistive technology does, by role and accessible name. getByText with a selector finds it too, but ties the test to the tag and skips the accessible-name check; test ids are the last resort, and a CSS class is an implementation detail that broke the old suite.

q: Before the customer clicks Pay, no error message must be shown. Which assertion is right?
options: expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
expect(screen.getAllByRole('alert')).toHaveLength(0)
expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
await expect(screen.findByRole('alert')).rejects.toThrow()
explain: queryBy returns null when nothing matches, so the negative assertion can run. getBy and getAllBy throw on zero matches before expect is even reached, so those tests fail. The findBy version works but waits a full second for nothing.

q: An input has an onChange handler. A test runs fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: 'mug' } }). How many times does the handler run?
options: Once, with the full value "mug"
Three times: "m", "mu", then "mug"
Zero: React ignores change events made by fireEvent
Four times: one per character plus one on blur
explain: fireEvent dispatches one change event with the final value (measured: one call with "mug", no keydown). user.type would call it three times, which is why a fireEvent test could not reveal a request per keystroke.

q: What does await screen.findByRole('alert') do when no alert ever appears?
options: It resolves to null at once, so the test can assert absence
It throws synchronously, like getByRole, before any retry
It waits until the test runner's own timeout, 5 s in Vitest
It retries, then rejects after 1,000 ms by default
explain: findBy queries retry until the element appears or their own timeout passes: measured, the promise rejected after 1,019 ms with "Unable to find role="alert"" and the DOM printed. Returning null is queryBy, and the 5 s Vitest timeout only matters if something never settles.

q: What does await waitFor(() => {}) check?
options: Nothing: an empty callback never throws
That React has finished all of its pending renders and effects
That no request started by the component is still in flight
That the DOM has stopped changing for one 50 ms interval
explain: waitFor resolves as soon as its callback stops throwing, and an empty callback never throws: measured, it resolved in 1 ms while the status was still "loading". It is not a "wait for React" helper; put the assertion you expect inside it, or use findBy.

q: How should MSW be organised for the storefront's component tests?
options: A new setupServer inside each test, listening and closing in that test, with only the handlers it needs
One server, happy-path handlers, server.use per error case, resetHandlers after each test
No handlers by default, with unhandled requests passed through to a staging Orders API
One handler set per file and no reset, since each test file already runs in its own worker
explain: Default happy-path handlers keep most tests short, server.use overrides one endpoint for one test, and resetHandlers removes that override so it cannot leak into the next test of the same file. Files are isolated from each other, but tests inside one file share the server.

q: Why does each test get its own QueryClient?
options: A QueryClient cannot be reused after its provider unmounts, so the second render throws
React StrictMode refuses a client that was created outside the component tree
MSW must register its handlers on each client separately, or requests are not intercepted
The client holds the cache, so a test could see data another test loaded
explain: Measured with the app's shared client and a 60 s staleTime: the second test made 0 requests and showed the first test's order. A client per test, built in the render helper, removes that coupling. The other reasons do not exist: MSW works at the network level, not per client.

q: A test calls vi.useFakeTimers(), then userEvent.setup() with no options, then await user.type(input, '10 rue'). What happens?
options: The text is typed instantly, because fake timers skip every delay
The text is typed, but the debounce timer fires after the first key
Typing stalls: user-event waits with setTimeout between keys
Vitest throws an error saying fake timers are not supported by user-event
explain: user-event waits between keystrokes with setTimeout, and fake timers only move when the test moves them: measured, not one character was typed after 2 s. The user-event docs say advanceTimers is necessary with fake timers: userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime }).

q: When should a custom hook get its own renderHook tests?
options: Always: every hook is a unit, and testing it through a component hides its failures
When several components share it and its contract has many cases
Never: renderHook was deprecated with React 19 and its test utilities
Only when the hook holds no state, since state needs a real component to render
explain: A shared hook with its own contract deserves direct tests at its boundaries. A hook written for one component is better tested through that component, as the Testing Library docs advise preferring render. renderHook is part of @testing-library/react 16, not deprecated.

q: Why did the Pay button snapshot stay green through the incident, then fail last week?
options: Snapshots ignore boolean attributes such as disabled, but they do compare whitespace
The snapshot file was never committed, so each CI run wrote a new one and passed
It held the first render only, and it compares markup, classes included
Snapshot serialisers only understand class components, not hooks
explain: A snapshot records the states the test reaches, and this one never clicked Pay. It compares serialised HTML, classes included: measured, renaming btn-primary produced a diff although nothing was broken. That pairing (misses the bug, fails on the refactor) is the usual case.

q: What does the last line do?
options: It returns the second input, because its placeholder becomes its accessible name
It returns the first input, the only textbox that has a label at all
It throws "Found multiple elements with the role "textbox"", as two inputs match
It throws "Unable to find an accessible element…": no textbox is named "Postcode"
explain: Testing Library computes an empty accessible name for an input with only a placeholder (measured: Name ""), so no textbox is named "Postcode" and getByRole throws. That is also a real accessibility bug: give the field a label. "Multiple elements" only happens without a name filter.

q: While the payment is in flight, the button reads "Paying…". What does each library do with a query for the name "Pay"?
options: Both match "Paying…", since both libraries compare names as case-insensitive substrings
Testing Library returns null; Playwright counts 1 unless exact: true
Neither matches: both compare whole, case-sensitive names unless told otherwise
Testing Library matches "Paying…"; Playwright returns 0 because it is strict
explain: Measured: Testing Library's string name matched the whole name, so queryByRole returned null, while Playwright's count was 1 and became 0 with exact: true. Playwright's docs say role names match a case-insensitive substring by default. Assuming the two libraries agree is how an E2E test passes on the wrong button.

q: What is the bug in this test?
options: waitFor re-runs the callback, so Pay is clicked several times
fireEvent cannot be called inside waitFor, so the callback throws every time
Nothing: the click runs once, and only the failing assertion is retried
getByRole inside waitFor never retries, so the status is read only once
explain: waitFor retries the callback on an interval and on DOM changes, side effects included: measured, Pay was clicked 5 times before the status appeared. Click once before waiting, then wait with findByRole('status'), which also makes a double payment visible instead of hidden.

q: A test prints "An update to OrderStatus inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)". It renders the page, sleeps 100 ms with setTimeout, then calls getByRole. Which fix would you ship?
options: Wrap the setTimeout in act() and keep the 100 ms sleep, which the warning asks for
Mock console.error in the setup file so CI logs stay clean and readable
Replace the sleep and getByRole with findByRole on the final state
Turn off the act environment flag for this file, since the result is correct anyway
explain: findBy waits for the state the user would see, inside Testing Library's act handling: measured, the same component produced no warning with findByText. Wrapping the sleep keeps a timing guess that is slow locally and short on CI, and silencing the warning or the flag hides the race.

q: In a Vitest project without globals: true and with no cleanup in the setup file, each test passes alone, but the second test of a file fails with "Found multiple elements with the role "button"". Why?
options: Vitest runs the tests of one file in parallel, so both render at the same time
Automatic cleanup needs a global afterEach, so the first test's DOM stays
jsdom cannot unmount React 19 roots, so every render adds to the same page
React 19 keeps every root alive until the test file ends, by design
explain: Testing Library registers cleanup only when afterEach is a global, as the docs say: measured, the previous test's element was still in the page. Turn on globals or call cleanup() in afterEach. Tests in one Vitest file run one after another, not in parallel.

q: With MSW 2 and onUnhandledRequest: 'error', a new component calls GET /cart, which has no handler. What happens in the test?
options: The request goes to the real network, and the test continues with whatever comes back
MSW answers with an empty 200 response, so the component renders an empty cart
MSW logs a warning, and the previous test's handler answers the request
MSW prints an error naming the request, and the fetch rejects
explain: Measured on MSW 2.15: "[MSW] Error: intercepted a request without a matching request handler" listed the method and URL, and fetch rejected. The forgotten mock fails visibly instead of hitting the network. In MSW 3 the option is onUnhandledFrame, and the old name is no longer read.

q: You need to assert that the button shows "Paying…" and is disabled while POST /orders is pending. Which approach is deterministic?
options: Hold the handler on a promise the test resolves after asserting
Add a 200 ms delay to the handler and assert within the first 200 ms of the click
Mock useMutation to return isPending: true for the whole test
Click Pay, sleep 50 ms so the request starts, then assert on the button
explain: A held response stays pending until the test releases it, so the in-flight state is checked with no timing at all (measured, then the paid status appeared after resolve). A delay or a sleep races the clock, and mocking useMutation no longer tests the component's real wiring.

q: A component renders an alert when its query fails. With new QueryClient() and a handler answering 500, await screen.findByRole('alert') fails. Why?
options: The 500 response is cached as a success, because its body is valid JSON
findBy cannot see elements that TanStack Query renders in a later batch
The query retries 3 times first, which outlasts findBy's timeout
MSW does not support 500 responses in Node, so the request hangs
explain: Queries retry failed requests 3 times by default with exponential backoff: measured, findBy gave up at 1,000 ms while the alert appeared after 7,082 ms and 4 requests. A test client with retry: false showed the alert after 22 ms and 1 request.

q: Both tests use the app's module-level queryClient (staleTime 60 s). Test 1 answers GET /orders/ord_1 with paid; test 2 overrides it with refunded. How many requests does test 2 make, and what does it show?
options: One request, because the handler changed; it shows "refunded"
Zero requests; it shows "paid" from test 1
One request; it shows "paid" first, then "refunded"
Two requests, because a remount refetches twice in tests
explain: The cached order is still fresh for 60 s, so the second mount uses it without a request: measured, 0 requests and "Order ord_1 is paid". Without staleTime it would refetch on mount, which is why this leak shows up only with some settings. A client per test removes it.

q: For the order status component, a colleague proposes vi.mock on the useOrder hook to return { data: order }. Which design would you ship?
options: The hook mock, because the tests become synchronous, fast and independent of the network
A vi.fn replacing fetch in each test, scripted with the order JSON
A real QueryClient per test and MSW handlers for the order
An E2E test only, since hooks that fetch data cannot run in jsdom
explain: With MSW and a real client the test runs the loading state, the error state and the cache, where the bugs live, and survives a switch from useQuery to useSuspenseQuery. The hook mock skips all of that and ties tests to an internal name; a fetch mock is the "mock what you do not own" mistake of M14.

q: Under Vitest, this test hits the 5 s test timeout. Why?
options: Testing Library waits for a setTimeout(0) it only advances under Jest
advanceTimers must be vi.runAllTimers, or the remaining keystrokes never fire
MSW cannot answer requests while fake timers are installed, so the query hangs
act cannot wrap an async function, so the debounce update is never applied
explain: Testing Library's asyncWrapper waits for a setTimeout(0) and only calls jest.advanceTimersByTime when it detects a jest global; under Vitest fake timers that timer never fires (measured: the test timed out). vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true }) fixed it. MSW kept answering in the passing version.

q: An axe scan of the checkout in CI reports zero violations. What can you conclude?
options: The checkout meets WCAG 2.1 AA, since those were the tags scanned
Screen reader users can complete the checkout from start to end
No accessibility work is needed until the checkout markup changes again
Only that axe found nothing it can detect; manual checks remain
explain: The Playwright docs state that automated scans catch common problems such as missing or invalid attributes, while many issues can only be found with manual testing. Zero violations is a useful gate in CI, not a conformance claim: focus order, meaningful names and flows need people.

q: What is result.current after the last line, and what else happens?
options: "10 rue de Rivoli", since the 300 ms have passed, with no warning
"10 r", plus an act(...) warning from React
undefined, because the cleanup cleared the timer and the state
It throws, because renderHook does not support fake timers
explain: The timer fired setDebounced outside act, so React had not rendered the update when the test read it: measured, result.current was still "10 r" and the act warning was printed. Wrapping the advance in act() gave "10 rue de Rivoli".

q: The storefront has a DOM snapshot for every component, and people update them with vitest -u without reading the diff. Which plan would you ship?
options: Run vitest -u automatically in CI, so that snapshots stop blocking merges for markup changes
Role-based assertions for behaviour, aria snapshots or screenshots for a few pages
Keep them all and add a review rule: every snapshot diff needs two approvals before merge
Convert every snapshot to toMatchInlineSnapshot, so reviewers see the HTML in the test file
explain: DOM snapshots miss behaviour they never reach and fail on harmless markup, so the fix is different assertions, not more process. Behaviour goes to role-based tests, structure to aria snapshots that ignore classes, and visuals to a few screenshots. Inlining large HTML only moves the noise into the test file.

q: This E2E line fails about once in twenty runs on CI. Why, and what is the fix?
code: expect(await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay', exact: true }).isEnabled()).toBe(true);
options: isEnabled() is deprecated and unreliable; read getAttribute('disabled') instead
The exact option makes name matching flaky on CI fonts; remove it
CI machines are slower; raise the global test timeout to 30 s
It reads once; use await expect(locator).toBeEnabled()
explain: isEnabled returns the state at that instant, so a button re-enabled a few milliseconds later fails the test on a slow runner. The web-first assertion retries until it passes or times out (5 s by default, measured in the failure output). A longer global timeout changes nothing for a one-shot read.

q: A developer adds await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png') and runs it on a Windows laptop, then pushes. CI runs on Linux. What happens?
options: Local run writes checkout-win32.png; CI has no Linux baseline
The first run passes and writes one baseline that every platform then shares
Playwright converts the Windows baseline to each platform when CI first runs it
The test is skipped on CI with a warning, because the platform differs from the baseline
explain: Measured on Playwright 1.64: the first run failed with "A snapshot doesn't exist … writing actual" and wrote checkout-win32.png. The platform in the name means a Linux run looks for a different file, and fonts render differently anyway, so generate baselines in the same environment as CI, such as its container.

q: With retries: 2, a checkout test fails once and passes on its first retry. With failOnFlakyTests off, what does Playwright report?
options: The test as failed, and the run fails
The test as passed, with no record of the failure
The test as flaky, and the run passes
The test as skipped after a failed attempt
explain: Measured on Playwright 1.64: a test that failed and then passed on retry was listed as "1 flaky" and the run passed. That is why the CI configuration of section 11 sets failOnFlakyTests: retries still give you a trace, but the flake no longer hides behind a green build.

q: An interviewer asks: "Your component tests were green, yet checkout broke twice. What do you change first?" Which answer shows senior judgment?
options: Raise the coverage threshold to 90% in CI, so that the untested error paths have to get tests
A user-level regression test per incident at the cheapest level, and drop the tests that hid them
Replace the component tests with Playwright E2E tests, since only a real browser shows what customers see
Add snapshots of the error and loading states, so that every state of checkout is covered next time
explain: Both bugs were behaviours no test reached: a component test with a 402 and one counting requests under fake timers would have caught them in milliseconds. Coverage counts executed lines, not meaningful assertions, an all-E2E suite is slow and flaky, and another snapshot repeats the original mistake.

q: Why does the design system's Button take variant: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger' rather than primary and danger booleans?
options: Booleans cannot be passed as props to a function component in React 19
It turns combinations like primary plus danger into type errors
A union is cheaper to compare than several booleans on each render
Boolean props would force the button to be a controlled component
explain: With two booleans, <Btn primary danger> compiles and describes a state no designer drew. A single union admits exactly one variant. Booleans are valid props in every React version, and neither choice has a measurable rendering cost.

q: Inside a <form>, an agent clicks <button>Refund</button>, which has no type attribute. What happens?
options: Nothing: a button without type does nothing until it has an onClick
The browser warns in the console and ignores the click
The form is submitted, because a button's default type is submit
The form is reset, because the default type is reset
explain: A button's default type is submit: measured in Chromium, clicking it fired the form's submit event and button.type read "submit". That is why the design system's Button defaults type to "button". A reset button needs type="reset" explicitly.

q: In <Tabs.Root><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab /></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel /></Tabs.Root>, how does a Tab know which value is selected?
options: It reads the selected value from a context that Root provides
Root clones each child element and injects the selected value as a prop
Each Tab keeps its own state and syncs it with an effect
The caller passes selected to every Tab by hand
explain: Root renders a context provider, and every part reads it with use (or useContext), however deep it sits. Cloning children only reaches direct children, so it breaks as soon as a Tab is wrapped in a List or a tooltip. Syncing local states with effects duplicates the state.

q: Which use of Tabs is controlled?
options: <Tabs.Root defaultValue="details">
<Tabs.Root defaultValue="details" onValueChange={track}>
<Tabs.Root> with each Tab marked selected
<Tabs.Root value={tab} onValueChange={setTab}>
explain: A component is controlled when the parent passes the value itself and stores changes, here value plus setTab. An onValueChange next to defaultValue only observes changes: the component still owns its state, so that use is uncontrolled.

q: What does a headless component library such as Radix, React Aria or Base UI give you?
options: Fully styled components in its own visual language, ready to theme
Behaviour and accessibility (ARIA, focus, keyboard) without styles
Design tokens and a Figma kit, but no components
Components that render only on the server
explain: Headless means unstyled: Base UI describes itself as "unstyled UI components for building accessible user interfaces", and Radix components "ship without styles". Styled libraries such as MUI are the ones that bring a visual language.

q: In a two-tier token system, which tokens should the Button's CSS use?
options: Raw hex values, so the button never depends on a theme
Primitive tokens such as --indigo-600
Semantic tokens such as --color-action
Whichever tier the designer used in the mock-up
explain: Components use semantic tokens, which name a role, and themes remap those roles to primitives. A button using --indigo-600 directly stays indigo 600 in dark mode, because the theme changes the semantic layer.

q: Why does the react.dev page on useInsertionEffect not recommend runtime <style> injection?
options: It makes the browser recalculate styles more often, and can be very slow
Injected styles are dropped by the browser as soon as hydration has finished
React 19 removed support for style elements rendered by components
Injected styles cannot read CSS custom properties defined in tokens
explain: The page gives those two reasons and recommends static CSS files for static styles plus inline styles for dynamic values. Injected styles do apply, and React 19 still renders style elements; the problem is cost, not correctness.

q: What is a Storybook play function?
options: A function that generates random args to fuzz-test the component
The function that renders the story on its documentation page
A script that records a video of the story for the designers
A story function that runs interactions after render and asserts
explain: Per the Storybook docs, a play function runs after the story renders: it can click, type and assert with expect, which makes the story an interaction test. Rendering is done by the story and its args; the play function adds behaviour on top.

q: The next @shop/ui release renames the Tabs prop onChange to onValueChange. Which version bump is correct?
options: Patch, because no new feature was added
Minor, because the new name is an addition
Major, because existing callers break
None, because TypeScript users will see the error anyway
explain: Semver reserves the major version for incompatible API changes, and a renamed prop breaks every caller using the old name. Shipping it as a patch is exactly the incident of section 8. A compile error is how users find out, not a reason to hide it in a patch.

q: In the feature-based back office, the refunds screen needs the order's total. What does the structure rule say?
options: Import OrdersTable from features/orders and read the total from its props
Compose both in the page under app, or fetch it through the API layer
Move the refunds feature inside features/orders
Copy the order types into features/refunds
explain: Features do not import each other; the app layer composes them, and shared data comes from the API layer. A cross-feature import is exactly what the lint rule forbids, and nesting or copying features only moves the coupling.

q: In the monorepo, apps/back-office depends on "@shop/ui": "workspace:*", and @shop/ui is at 2.3.0. What happens to that range when a package that depends on @shop/ui is published?
options: pnpm replaces it with the exact version, 2.3.0
pnpm publishes it as is, and consumers need pnpm to install it
pnpm replaces it with latest
pnpm refuses to publish a package with a workspace dependency
explain: The pnpm docs say workspace:* becomes the exact version of the local package when packing or publishing (and workspace:^ becomes ^2.3.0). So consumers outside the monorepo see an ordinary semver range.

q: For a 10% rollout of the new orders table, why should the flag be evaluated with the agent id as the targeting key?
options: Flag services refuse to evaluate a flag without a user id attached
It makes the flag service answer faster thanks to its cache
It lets each agent switch tables from their settings page
The same agent gets the same table every visit, so groups compare
explain: The targeting key identifies the subject the flag is evaluated for, so a stable key keeps each agent in one group: the experience is consistent and the metrics of the two groups mean something. A random or per-page-load decision would flip agents between tables. The key is about consistency, not speed or permission.

q: A caller renders <LeakyButton className="wide">Refund</LeakyButton>. What is the class attribute of the rendered button?
options: "ui-button wide", because React merges the className values it receives
"ui-button", because the explicit attribute wins
"wide": the spread comes last and replaces the base class
Both classes, in the order "wide ui-button"
explain: JSX props are applied in order, and the later className from rest overwrites the earlier one: measured with React 19.3.1, the button rendered class="wide" and lost its base styles. React never merges class names; destructure className and join it with the base class.

q: With React 19.3.1, after this renders, what is closeRef.current?
options: null: ref is a plain prop, and IconButton never uses it
The <button> element, because React attaches refs to the first DOM node
The component instance, as with class components
React throws, because function components need forwardRef
explain: In React 19, ref reaches a function component as a prop, and nothing attaches it unless the component puts it on an element: measured, ref.current stayed null. React does not throw anymore; forwardRef is no longer necessary, but forwarding still has to be written.

q: The checkout form renders <OrderButton type="submit">Place order</OrderButton>. What happens on click?
options: The form is submitted, because the caller asked for submit
React warns about a duplicate prop and submits the form
The form is submitted twice, once per type attribute
Nothing: the later type="button" overrides the caller
explain: Props written after the spread win, so the rendered button has type="button": measured, the form's submit handler was called 0 times. That is right for a default and wrong for a forced value; put the default in the destructuring (type = 'button') so callers can override it.

q: A teammate creates the Tabs context with a default object, createContext({ selected: '', select: () => {} }), to "avoid null checks". What changes when someone renders <Tabs.Tab> outside <Tabs.Root>?
options: Nothing changes, because React throws in both versions anyway
It renders, clicks do nothing, and the bug ships silently
The tab silently creates its own Root and works on its own
TypeScript rejects the JSX at compile time with a context error
explain: With a default value, use returns the default outside a provider: measured, the tab rendered with aria-selected="false" and clicking changed nothing. With null and a guard, the same mistake throws "<Tabs.Tab> must be rendered inside <Tabs.Root>" during development. TypeScript cannot see where a component is rendered.
