q: The first Tabs used hard-coded ids: id={'tab-' + value} and aria-controls={'panel-' + value}. The order detail page now shows Tabs in the main area and in a customer side panel, both with a details tab. What breaks, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing breaks: ids only need to be unique inside one component tree
React detects duplicate ids and renames the second set automatically
Duplicate ids point ARIA to the wrong panel; prefix them with useId
The second Tabs fails to render until it gets its own separate Root
explain: Ids must be unique in the whole document, and assistive technology follows aria-controls and aria-labelledby to the first match. useId gives each instance its own prefix: measured, two instances got _r_1_-tab-details and _r_2_-tab-details. React does not rewrite ids.

q: An agent clicks the Refunds tab. What happens?
options: track is called with "refunds", and the Details panel stays visible
The Refunds panel shows, and track is called with "refunds" as well
The Refunds panel shows, but the track callback is never called
React throws, because value needs a matching useState
explain: Passing value makes the Tabs controlled, so it shows what the parent says, and this parent always says "details". Measured: the callback received "refunds" and the Details panel stayed. Fix it by storing the tab in state and passing it back, or by using defaultValue if the parent only observes.

q: The order detail first renders <Tabs.Root defaultValue="details">. When the order loads and turns out to be refunded, it re-renders with defaultValue="refunds". Which panel shows?
options: Refunds, because the new defaultValue resets the state
Refunds, but only after a second render triggered by React
Neither: React throws when a default changes
Details: defaultValue is only read on the first render
explain: defaultValue seeds useState, which ignores later initial values: measured, the Details panel stayed. To start on Refunds, render Tabs after the order loads, give it a key that changes with the order, or control it with value.

q: The page first renders <Tabs.Root value="refunds" defaultValue="details">, then re-renders without the value prop (the ?tab parameter was removed). With the useControllableState hook of section 3, which panel shows?
options: Refunds, because the hook remembers the last controlled value it saw
Details: the internal state was never updated while controlled
No panel, because the selected value becomes undefined
Payments, the next tab in the list
explain: While controlled, the hook never writes its internal state, which still holds the initial "details"; once value is gone it reads that state. Measured with React 19.3.1: the Details panel showed. That is why a component should stay controlled or uncontrolled for its whole life; for an <input>, React 19 warns "A component is changing a controlled input to be uncontrolled" (measured).

q: The refund confirmation is built on Base UI's Dialog with default options. The agent presses Escape. What happens to focus?
options: Focus stays on the last focused element inside the closed dialog
Focus moves to the top of the document
The dialog closes and focus returns to the Refund button
Escape is ignored until the agent clicks Cancel
explain: The Base UI docs say a modal dialog traps Tab inside, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the trigger or the previously focused element by default. Focus restoration is exactly the kind of behaviour that hand-made dialogs forget, which is the main argument for a headless primitive.

q: A team writes <Dialog.Trigger render={<BrandButton />}>Refund</Dialog.Trigger>, with function BrandButton({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return <button className="brand">{children}</button>; }. What is wrong?
options: BrandButton drops the props and ref Base UI passes to it
Nothing: Base UI attaches its handlers to the DOM node after render
The render prop only accepts native elements such as button
The label must be passed to BrandButton, not to Dialog.Trigger
explain: The Base UI docs state that the custom component must forward the ref and spread all received props on its DOM node; BrandButton ignores them, so the click handler, ARIA attributes and ref never reach the button. The section 1 Button, which spreads rest including ref, meets the requirement.

q: To darken one panel, a developer writes .panel { --gray-900: #f9fafb; }. What colour is the text of a <p> inside the panel?
options: #f9fafb, because the closest --gray-900 declaration always wins
#111827: --color-text was resolved on :root and inherited
The initial colour, because the variable reference is circular
It depends on which rule comes later in the file
explain: A custom property's var() is substituted on the element where it is declared, and descendants inherit the result. Measured in Chromium: the text stayed rgb(17, 24, 39). Redefine --color-text in the panel or theme scope instead of the primitive.

q: With the tokens file of section 5, an agent's OS is in dark mode and the back office sets <html data-theme="light"> from the agent's saved choice. What does the page use?
options: Dark tokens, because the media query is more specific than the attribute
Dark tokens, until the agent reloads the page
A mix of both: dark surface and light text
Light: the dark block no longer matches, so the :root values apply
explain: The dark media block applies only when data-theme is not "light", so the explicit choice wins. Measured in Chromium with emulated dark mode: text stayed rgb(17, 24, 39). Without the :not() guard, the media query would override the saved choice.

q: The storefront team wants @shop/ui styled with styled-components and its ThemeProvider, as their old code was. In Next.js App Router Server Components, which statement is true?
options: styled-components cannot render in Server Components, in any version
ThemeProvider works exactly the same in Server and Client Components
It renders there, but ThemeProvider is a pass-through: no context
Next.js converts ThemeProvider themes to CSS variables automatically
explain: The styled-components docs state native React Server Components support since 6.3, with ThemeProvider as a pass-through ("no context in RSC") and themes moved to CSS custom properties. Next.js documents React context as unsupported in Server Components. So themes must be CSS variables anyway, and static CSS is the simpler choice for a shared package.

q: A refactor of button.module.css moves the focus outline under a neighbouring element. Interaction and accessibility tests all pass. Which test would have caught it?
options: A visual test comparing snapshots with approved baselines
A play function that tabs to the button and asserts it has focus
The a11y addon configured with test: 'error' in preview.ts
A TypeScript type check on the Button component props
explain: The element still receives focus and the markup is still valid, so interaction and axe checks pass; only the pixels changed. Visual tests (Chromatic, in Storybook's docs) compare snapshots with baselines and flag the change for review. That is why each layer of testing covers a different risk.

q: The partner portal broke after a patch release renamed onChange to onValueChange. Which plan would you ship to fix the process?
options: Ask the agency to pin exact versions and stop upgrading the package
Restore onChange as deprecated, remove it in the next major
Keep the rename and publish a blog post that explains the change
Move the partner portal into the monorepo so it gets changes at once
explain: Fix the semver contract: bring the old prop back marked @deprecated with a development warning, then remove it in a major whose changeset explains the migration. Pinning forever stops all fixes, and the agency's repository is not yours to move.

q: CI fails on import { OrdersTable } from '../orders/orders-table' inside src/features/refunds. The refunds page needs to show the order lines. Which fix would you ship?
options: Add ./orders to the except list of the refunds zone in the config
Disable the rule for that line with an eslint-disable comment
Copy orders-table.tsx into features/refunds and adapt it
Compose both features in the page, or use the shared DataTable
explain: The rule exists so features stay independent; the page layer is where features meet, and a generic table belongs in the design system. Widening except or disabling the rule reintroduces the coupling that broke the customers page, and a copy drifts.

q: The agency proposes Module Federation so its partner screens load inside the back office at runtime. One back-office team ships weekly, and partners use their own portal. What do you answer?
options: Yes: Module Federation is the standard way to share a design system
Yes, and mark React as non-shared so each part gets its own copy
No: keep the portal a separate app using the published packages
No, because Module Federation only works with Next.js apps
explain: Micro-frontends pay off when several teams must deploy parts of the same page independently; here the portal is its own app, so a package is enough. Two copies of React cause the invalid hook call error (react.dev), which is why federated React must be a shared singleton. Module Federation works with Webpack and Rspack and lists Vite and Next.js integrations.

q: Which flag design would you ship for the new orders table?
options: A flag checked in each column and cell component, so each part can be rolled out alone
One page-level flag, default false, keyed by agent id, with an end date
A flag read once at build time from an environment variable
One flag per agent, created by hand in the flag service
explain: One page-level flag keeps two tested states, the safe default protects agents if the flag service fails, the agent id keeps groups stable, and an end date gets the flag and the old table deleted. Per-cell flags multiply untested combinations, and a build-time variable cannot be rolled back without a redeploy.

q: In the RADIO method, what does the I step produce?
options: The component tree, with the state each component owns and the events that flow between them.
The APIs between components and with the server: names, parameters, return values.
The list of optimisations, ordered by their expected effect on the Core Web Vitals of the page.
The core entities and their fields, each marked as coming from the server or the client.
explain: I is the Interface definition: the endpoints and the component props, with their parameters and return values. The component tree is the Architecture step and the entities are the Data model step, which is why the first and last options are tempting.

q: According to the GreatFrontEnd playbook, roughly how much of the session should go to optimisations and the deep dive?
options: About 10%, the cap for requirements
About 20%, like the architecture
About 25%, a quarter of the round
About 40%
explain: The playbook gives roughly 40% to the O step, the largest share, because the deep dive is where seniority shows. 10% is the cap it gives to requirements, and 20% is the share of architecture and of the interface.

q: Why does the suggestions API return matched character ranges instead of a label with <mark> tags already in it?
options: So the client builds the marks as text: no server markup is ever inserted as HTML.
Ranges are smaller than HTML, which matters because HTTP/2 compresses headers but not bodies.
A CDN refuses to cache JSON responses that contain HTML tags, so the list would never be cached.
ARIA forbids any child element inside role="option", so a mark would break the pattern.
explain: Inserting server HTML means dangerouslySetInnerHTML, a cross-site scripting risk; ranges let React render text and <mark> elements safely. CDNs cache JSON regardless of its content, and options may contain elements, as the APG examples do.

q: The customer types chair with keystrokes 80 ms apart, and the hook debounces by 250 ms. How many suggestion requests were sent in the jsdom measurement?
options: Five, one per keystroke
Two, for ch and chair
One, for chair
None until the input loses focus
explain: Each keystroke resets the 250 ms timer, so the term only settles after the last one: one request, for chair. Two requests would need a pause longer than the delay in the middle of the word.

q: Which question of the caching checklist says that personal recent searches must never be served with Cache-Control: public?
options: Freshness
Scope
Lifetime
Version
explain: Scope asks who may share an entry: public suggestions can be shared by everyone at the CDN, personal data must not be. Freshness and lifetime are about time, not about who sees the entry.

q: In the APG combobox pattern, where is DOM focus while the customer moves through the suggestions with the arrow keys?
options: On the input, while aria-activedescendant points to the active option.
On the active option, moved there with focus() on each arrow key press.
On the listbox, which needs tabindex="0" so that it can receive the arrow keys.
On the document body, until the customer presses Enter to pick an option.
explain: The APG says DOM focus stays on the combobox; assistive technology follows aria-activedescendant. Moving real focus to the option would stop the customer from typing, which is why the second option is wrong despite being a common implementation.

q: Why do the filters and the sort of the orders table live in the URL?
options: Because the server can only render a table from query parameters, never from a request body.
Because TanStack Query needs the URL as its query key to cache each view of the table separately.
Because React state is lost on every re-render of the table, while the URL survives re-renders.
So an agent can share a link, reload, and use the back button without losing the view.
explain: The URL makes the view shareable, reloadable and part of the history. TanStack Query takes any serialisable key, not the URL, and React state survives re-renders; it is lost on reload, which is the point of the URL.

q: Measured in Chromium, changing one cell of a 5,000-row table re-laid out the table in 110 to 180 ms. Why does virtualisation fix this?
options: It moves the layout work to a worker thread, so the main thread stays free for input.
It draws the rows on a canvas, which the browser does not need to lay out at all.
Only the visible rows exist in the DOM, so layout handles about 50 rows.
It switches the table to table-layout: fixed, which skips measuring cell contents.
explain: Layout cost follows the number of elements, and virtualisation keeps only the visible rows: the 50-row table re-laid out in under 10 ms. table-layout: fixed alone still took 30 to 45 ms at 5,000 rows, and layout never runs in a worker.

q: 100 status events arrive 5 ms apart. Written to the query cache one by one, they caused 96 commits of the table. How many with a buffer flushed every 250 ms, in the same measurement?
explain: The events spread over about half a second, so a 250 ms flush applies them in a handful of batches: 7 commits, counting the first renders. One commit would need all events in a single flush.

q: Which back office action is a good fit for an optimistic update?
options: Refunding 50 € to a customer.
Assigning an order to yourself.
Deleting a customer account.
Cancelling a shipped order with the carrier.
explain: Optimistic updates suit actions that nearly always succeed and are cheap to undo on screen. A refund, a deletion or a carrier cancellation has consequences the agent must see confirmed, so they show a pending state and wait.

q: Which props should the main product photo get with next/image in Next.js 16?
options: priority, which preloads the image and marks it as the LCP element.
loading="lazy" with a blur placeholder, so the page shell paints first.
preload and fetchPriority="high" together, for the strongest hint to the browser.
loading="eager" and fetchPriority="high", plus width and height.
explain: web.dev says never lazy-load the LCP image and recommends high fetch priority; next/image lazy-loads by default, hence loading="eager". priority is deprecated since Next.js 16, and the docs list "when fetchPriority is used" among the cases where preload should not be.

q: When should the storefront create a new idempotency key for POST /orders?
options: On every click of Place order, so each click is a distinct request.
On every automatic retry, so the server can tell the attempts apart.
When the intent changes, such as a new cart version.
Once per browser session, stored in localStorage so a reload keeps it.
explain: The key identifies one intent: retries and second clicks must reuse it so the server replays the first answer. A new key per click or per retry defeats the purpose, and one key per session would make the server replay an old order for a new cart.

q: The customer types ch, then cha; the ch request is the slower one. What can this component end up showing?
options: The results for ch: its answer arrives last and overwrites the answer for cha.
Always the results for cha: React ignores state updates from an effect that has re-run.
An error: React throws when state is set after the effect re-ran.
Both lists merged, because setResults is batched.
explain: Measured with React 19.3 in jsdom: the naive component showed the ch results after cha was typed. React does not discard updates from an old effect; you need a cleanup flag, an abort, or data keyed by term as with TanStack Query.

q: With useSuggestions (signal passed to fetch), the customer types ch, then cha before ch answers, waits for cha's list, then deletes back to ch. What happens on the way back to ch?
options: ch is served from the cache with no request, because it was requested a few seconds earlier.
The list keeps showing the results for cha until the debounce timer fires for ch again.
A new request: the first was cancelled, and a cancelled query reverts to its empty state.
The query moves to an error state and the customer sees an AbortError message under the box.
explain: TanStack Query reverts a cancelled query to its previous state, here empty, so ch was requested again in the measurement while cha was served from the cache. The cancellation is not reported as an error, which rules out the last option.

q: A colleague removes signal from the query function. ch is slower than cha. What did the jsdom measurement show?
options: ch's results flashed on screen for a moment, then cha's results replaced them.
cha's results; the late ch answer was stored under its own key.
ch's results, because its answer arrived last and replaced the cha entry.
Nothing at all until both requests had finished, then cha's results.
explain: Keying by term is what prevents the race: the component reads the cha entry, and the late ch answer only fills its own entry. The signal saves bandwidth and connections; it is not what keeps the screen correct.

q: The interviewer asks: "After launch, how do you know the autocomplete is good?" Which answer is the senior one?
options: A Lighthouse performance score above 90, checked in CI on every pull request that touches search.
The number of React renders per keystroke, read from the Profiler in a production build.
The CPU usage and p99 latency of the search service during the evening peak hour.
Field data: keystroke-to-list time, share of searches ending on a suggestion, errors, INP at p75.
explain: Requirements were stated as user experience, so the measures are field data from real sessions that map to them. Lighthouse is a lab check on one machine and renders per keystroke are a means; neither tells you whether customers find products faster.

q: In Chromium, the list is open in this <input type="search"> and the customer presses Escape once. What happens?
options: The list closes and the browser also clears the text.
The list closes and the text stays, which is what the APG expects from a combobox.
Nothing happens, because Escape is not delivered to keydown handlers in a search input.
The list closes and the surrounding form is submitted with the current text.
explain: Measured with Playwright 1.64: Escape in a search input cleared the field. Calling event.preventDefault() while the list is open makes the first Escape only close it, and leaves the second to clear the field.

q: A mouse click on a suggestion picks nothing: the list just closes. The input closes the list in onBlur, and options only have onClick. What is the bug?
options: Options need tabindex="0", otherwise the browser does not deliver clicks to list items.
React does not fire onClick on elements that carry role="option", only on buttons and links.
mousedown blurs the input, and onBlur removes the list before click fires.
aria-selected must be true before an option can be clicked, so the first click only selects.
explain: Measured in Chromium: without the mousedown guard nothing was picked; with it, mouse clicks and touch taps picked the option. Adding tabindex would make it worse, since the option would take focus away from the input.

q: Agents filter 2 million orders by status and sort them by amount. Where should filtering and sorting run?
options: In the browser, after loading every order once into IndexedDB for instant sorting.
On the server, with the parameters in the URL and the query key.
In a web worker, so the main thread stays free while it sorts the 2 million rows.
In the memory of the BFF, refreshed every minute from the Orders API.
explain: Millions of rows cannot be downloaded to each agent, so the database, with its indexes, filters and sorts. A worker only moves the cost of data the client should not hold, and a BFF copy is a stale second database.

q: What does this call return with the OrdersSearch schema of section 5 (Zod 4.6)?
code: readOrdersSearch(new URLSearchParams('status=lost&sort=hack'));
options: It throws a ZodError with two issues.
{ status: 'lost', sort: 'hack' }, because URL values are not checked.
{}, because invalid fields are removed and defaults are ignored.
An object with status: undefined and sort: '-createdAt'.
explain: Each field has .catch(), so an invalid value falls back: no status, and the default sort. Without .catch() the parse would throw, which is what you do not want for a link someone typed or edited by hand.

q: A first draft of the batch function looked like this. What goes wrong?
options: Map does not keep insertion order, so the events of a batch are applied in a random order.
setQueriesData only updates the first query that matches the key, not every view of the list.
An older event after a newer one in the same batch wins, and the row goes stale.
Rows without an event throw, because latest.get returns undefined for orders not in the batch.
explain: A map built from pairs keeps the last pair per key, so arrival order wins over version: measured, the row went back to an old status. Keep the highest version per order instead. Undefined is handled by the event && check, so the last option does not happen.

q: Your per-event version rendered 3 times for 100 events in the demo, and 96 times in production. Why?
options: The demo events came in one burst and were batched; spread out, each one rendered.
Production builds of React turn automatic batching off to keep each update predictable.
EventSource groups the events of a stream together in development builds only.
StrictMode renders every component twice in production, which doubles the commits.
explain: Measured in Chromium: the same code committed about 3 times for a burst and 96 times for events 5 ms apart. React batches updates that land together, not updates spread over separate tasks; StrictMode double rendering happens in development only.

q: Why does onMutate call cancelQueries before writing the optimistic row?
options: To abort the mutation itself if the agent navigates away before the server answers.
So a refetch in flight cannot land later and overwrite the optimistic row.
Because setQueryData throws an error while a query with the same key is fetching.
To empty the cache, so that the next render reads the list from the server again.
explain: TanStack Query's guide cancels outgoing refetches "so they don't overwrite our optimistic update". setQueryData works during a fetch; the problem is that the older server answer would arrive later and win.

q: The orders table now has editable status and assignee cells, and it is virtualised. Which accessibility design fits?
options: A native table with every cell and every control in the tab order, in reading order.
role="grid" with tabindex="0" on every cell, so the Tab key reaches each cell in turn.
aria-live="assertive" on each row, so every change is announced as soon as it happens.
The APG grid: one tab stop, arrow keys, aria-sort, aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex.
explain: The APG grid pattern is meant for interactive tabular data and has one tab stop, with arrow keys inside. Putting every cell in the tab order makes a table of hundreds of cells unusable with a keyboard, and assertive live regions on every row would interrupt constantly.

q: Product pages must be indexable, have a fast LCP, and show current stock. Which design would you ship?
options: Tagged product data in the static shell, revalidated on change; stock and cart per request in Suspense.
Client-side rendering with TanStack Query for every part, so the stock and the price are always fresh.
Full server rendering on every request with no cache at all, so every part of the page is always current.
Every product prerendered at build time, and the whole site rebuilt every night with the new catalogue.
explain: Shared content cached and revalidated on change gives HTML for search engines and a CDN-fast shell, while the parts that must be current stream per request. Client rendering hurts indexing and LCP, rendering everything per request makes every visit pay for the slowest data, and nightly builds leave prices wrong for hours.

q: Marketing wants an A/B test on the Buy button of the product page. Which design?
options: Render variant A, read the cookie in useEffect, and swap the button to variant B when needed.
Pick a random variant in the Server Component on every request, without storing anything.
Assign it in proxy.ts with a cookie, render it on the server, key the cache by variant.
Hide the button with CSS until the A/B testing script has loaded, then show the right one.
explain: Server assignment avoids flicker and layout shift, the cookie keeps each customer in one variant, and keying the cache by variant keeps one shell per variant. Random assignment per request moves customers between variants, which ruins the test.

q: Analytics events are lost when customers switch apps on their phones. Which fix?
options: Send them with fetch inside an unload handler, which runs when the page is closed.
Flush them with navigator.sendBeacon when visibilitychange reports the page hidden.
Send them with a synchronous XMLHttpRequest in beforeunload so they cannot be dropped.
Await a fetch for every event as it happens, so nothing is left in memory to lose.
explain: MDN calls visibilitychange the most reliable moment and sendBeacon the API made for it. unload and beforeunload often never fire on mobile, and unload also keeps the page out of the back/forward cache.

q: With PlaceOrderButton as written (disabled={placeOrder.isPending}), what did a double-click send in Chromium?
options: One request, because the disabled button blocked the second click before it fired.
Two requests carrying two different keys, so the server created two orders.
No request at all, because the second click cancelled the first mutation.
Two requests with the same idempotency key, so the server creates one order.
explain: isPending reached the button only after the second click, so two POSTs left, both with the key created by the first click. That is why the key, checked by the server, is the guarantee and the disabled state is only comfort.

q: A feed creates its IntersectionObserver once, on mount. The first page is 100 px tall in a 900 px viewport. What happens?
options: One page loads, then nothing: the sentinel never stops intersecting, so no new callback.
Pages load one after another, each time the callback runs, until the sentinel leaves the viewport.
An endless loop of requests, because the sentinel is always intersecting the viewport.
The observer throws an error, because the sentinel element moved after the first page.
explain: An observer reports changes in intersection, not states: measured in Chromium, the long-lived observer fired once and the list stopped at 100 px. Recreating it after each page reports the current state again, and the feed then filled the screen.

q: Twelve new items are published while the customer reads the feed. What do you do?
options: Insert them at the top at once: customers expect a live feed.
Show a "Show 12 new items" button and insert them when clicked.
Reload the whole feed every minute so it stays current.
Insert them at the top, then scroll down by their height in a timeout.
explain: Inserting above the reader moves the content she is reading and counts against CLS. web.dev excludes shifts within 500 ms of a click from CLS, so inserting on her click is both polite and free; compensating the scroll in a timeout still flickers and is fragile.

q: The 60-minute React round on the orders table begins. What is the best use of the first five minutes?
options: Start typing the component at once, and explain the design later if there is time left
Restate the task, ask two or three questions, and say the plan: a working version first
Set up a global store and a design system first, so that the code scales with the features
Write the complete test suite before any component code, as strict TDD would require
explain: The scorecard grades clarifying and planning before anything else, and a plan that reaches working code early. Starting at once is the tempting answer, but it hides your reasoning and often builds the wrong thing. A store or a full test suite up front spends the round on setup instead of a working feature.

q: Why does promiseAll store each result with results[index] = result instead of results.push(result)?
options: Because push is slower than index assignment once the array has more than a few items
Because push throws on an array that was created with new Array(n) and has empty slots
Because push follows the completion order, and the result must follow the input order
Because TypeScript cannot infer the element type when push is called on a generic array
explain: Promise.all fulfils with results in the order of the inputs, whatever order they finish in. push appends in completion order, so a slow first promise ends up last. push works fine on such an array and is not meaningfully slower; the problem is the order.

q: In the Emitter of section 3, why does emit not copy the listener array before looping over it?
options: Because on, once and off replace the array instead of mutating it, so emit holds a snapshot
Because for...of takes a copy of the array before the first iteration, so changes are safe
Because a listener cannot call off while an emit is running, so the array cannot change
Because private class fields are frozen for the duration of a method call on the instance
explain: off uses toSpliced and on uses a spread, both of which create new arrays, so the loop keeps iterating the old one. for...of does not copy: it reads the live array, which is why a mutating implementation needs a copy. Listeners can and do call off during an emit, which is exactly the case this design handles.

q: A search box uses debounce(search, 300). The user types "r", "re" and "red" within 200 ms, then stops. What happens?
options: Three searches, one per keystroke, each 300 ms after its keystroke
One search for "r", because the first call wins
One search for "red", 300 ms after the first keystroke
One search for "red", 300 ms after the last keystroke
explain: Each call clears the pending timer and starts a new one with the latest arguments, so only the last call survives, 300 ms after it. Counting from the first keystroke is the tempting mistake: that would be closer to a throttle with a trailing call. The test of section 4 checks exactly this with mock timers.

q: Why do the workers of mapWithLimit share one items.entries() iterator?
options: Because an iterator runs each of its items on a separate thread, which gives real parallelism
Because each next() hands out one item and its index exactly once, so no item is taken twice
Because Promise.all only accepts iterators, and an array would make it run sequentially
Because a shared iterator makes the results come back in completion order, which is faster
explain: The shared iterator is the queue: whichever worker is free takes the next item, and the index tells it where to store the result, which keeps the input order. Iterators do not create threads; JavaScript runs one worker at a time and they interleave at each await.

q: The interviewer asks for deepClone of an order that holds a Date, a Map and a reference to itself. What is the best first answer?
options: Name structuredClone, which keeps Date, Map and cycles, then write it by hand only if asked
Use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(order)), which keeps Dates, Maps and nested objects intact
Use the spread operator, which copies nested objects and Maps along with the top level
Use Object.assign({}, order), which follows the self-reference and copies it once, safely
explain: Measured on Node 24, structuredClone kept the Date, the Map and the cycle, and threw DataCloneError on a function. A JSON round trip turns the Date into a string, drops undefined and throws on a cycle. Spread and Object.assign copy only the first level.

q: Why does OrdersTable compute its rows with selectOrders during render instead of storing them in state from an effect?
options: Because an effect is not allowed to call setState, so the rows could never be stored there
Because useState cannot hold arrays of more than a few hundred items without slowing down
Because the props stay the single source of truth: no stale copy and no extra render
Because code that runs during render is moved to a worker thread by React 19 automatically
explain: Derived data belongs in render: a copy in state can fall out of sync with the props and arrives one render late. Effects can call setState, which is precisely the pattern that causes the extra render. Render runs on the main thread like everything else.

q: What does dialog.showModal() give you that a div with role="dialog" does not?
options: Only a nicer default style and a backdrop; focus and keyboard handling are still up to you
A focus trap and Escape handling, but focus is not returned to the opener after closing
Server-side rendering of the dialog content, so it appears before the JavaScript loads
Focus moved inside, an inert page behind, Escape to close, focus returned to the opener
explain: Measured in Chromium, showModal focused the first button, kept Tab and clicks away from the page behind, closed on Escape, and returned focus to the Refund button. A div with a role only announces itself as a dialog; all of that behaviour would be yours to write.

q: Which states should the fetch-and-display take-home handle before the reviewers open it?
options: Only data, because the API is reliable in the exercise
Loading, error with a way to retry, empty, and data
Loading and data; errors belong in the console
Data and a 404 page
explain: Reviewers check the unhappy states first: what a user sees while waiting, when the request fails, and when there is nothing to show. Logging errors to the console leaves the user with a blank or frozen screen and no way to retry.

q: In the reviewed OrderNotes, the list displays in the right order. Why is notes.sort(...) still a bug?
options: sort reorders the array in place, and that array belongs to the parent or the query cache
sort returns undefined, so the state is set to undefined and the list renders nothing
sort cannot compare ISO date strings with localeCompare, so the order is only approximate
sort runs asynchronously on large arrays and may finish after React has rendered the list
explain: Array.prototype.sort mutates and returns the same array, so the component changes data it does not own; the reproduction showed the parent's array reordered. sort does return the array, which is why the bug looks harmless. toSorted returns a sorted copy.

q: The Pay button does nothing on click and the console is clean. What does document.elementFromPoint(x, y) at the button's position tell you?
options: Whether the button has a click listener attached, and which function the listener calls
The list of CSS rules that apply to the button, including the ones that were overridden
Which element actually receives a click at that point, for example an invisible overlay
Whether the button is disabled, either by its own attribute or by a parent fieldset
explain: elementFromPoint returns the topmost element that hit-testing finds at that position. In the reproduction it returned a transparent toast region covering the page, which is why the click never reached the button. Listeners and styles are inspected in DevTools, not with this call.

q: In the AI-allowed round, the assistant writes the suggestion list with <div onClick> items. What do you do?
options: Accept it as it is, since the existing tests pass and the interviewer wants to see speed
Ask the assistant to add a comment that explains why a div was used instead of a button
Delete the generated code and rewrite all of it by hand, without explaining the decision
Say why it fails keyboard users, ask for the APG pattern, review it, add a keyboard test
explain: The grade is how you direct and check the assistant: name the defect, give it the right context, review its output aloud and prove the behaviour with a test. Passing tests do not prove accessibility if they never use the keyboard. Rewriting silently hides the skill being graded.

q: A candidate writes this Promise.all. What does the last line print?
options: [ 'price', 'stock' ]
[ 'stock' ]
[ 'stock', 'price' ]
Nothing: the promise never resolves
explain: push records results in completion order: "stock" is ready at once, "price" after 20 ms. Run on Node 24, it printed [ 'stock', 'price' ], while the native Promise.all printed [ 'price', 'stock' ]. Storing by index fixes it.

q: Another version stores results by index and resolves when a counter reaches 0, but has no check for an empty list. What happens with await promiseAll([])?
options: It never settles: forEach runs no callback, so nothing ever calls resolve
It resolves with an empty array, exactly like the native Promise.all does for an empty list
It rejects with a TypeError, because the counter starts at zero and goes below it
It resolves with undefined, because the results array never receives an element
explain: The counter is only checked inside the then callbacks, and an empty list has none. Run on Node 24, that version was still pending after 100 ms, while Promise.all([]) fulfilled with []. The early return for an empty list is part of the answer.

q: What does this print in a browser?
options: ['first', 'second', 'dup', 'dup']
['first', 'second', 'dup']
['first', 'dup', 'dup']
['first', 'dup']
explain: Measured in Chromium: a DOM EventTarget skips a listener removed during dispatch, and ignores a second registration of the same function. The first option is what Node's EventEmitter gives with the equivalent code (also measured), which is why you state your emitter's semantics.

q: What is the bug in this once, given that off removes by identity?
options: The wrapper runs twice on the first emit, because off is called while the loop is running
off compares with showToast, but the list holds the wrapper, so the toast still shows once
The arrow function loses this, so this.off throws a TypeError on the first emit
once must return a promise that resolves on the first event, or the listener leaks
explain: The registered function is the wrapper, so off(event, showToast) finds nothing; run on Node 24, the listener still fired once. Store the original function next to a once flag, as section 3 does, or keep a map from original to wrapper. Arrow functions keep this from once, so this.off works.

q: How many times does this component call searchProducts when the user types "red"?
options: Three times, for "r", "re" and "red": each render creates a new debounced function
Once, for "red", 300 ms after the last keystroke, which is what debounce is for
Once, for "r", because the first debounced call wins and the later ones are dropped
Never, because each state update re-renders the component and that cancels the timer
explain: Each keystroke re-renders, and each render builds a fresh debounce whose timer nobody clears. Measured with React 19.3.1 and user-event: three calls. Creating the debounced function once (a useState initializer or a ref) gave one call for "red". Nothing in React cancels a timer for you.

q: With the debounce of section 4, what does saved contain at the end of this test?
explain: "a" and "b" are each replaced before 300 ms pass; "c" gets its full 300 ms and runs; "d" has waited only 100 ms when the test ends. Run with node:test on Node 24, saved was ['c']. Answering ['a', 'c'] confuses debounce with a leading throttle.

q: To refund orders 3 at a time, a colleague cuts the list into chunks of 3 and awaits Promise.all per chunk. The tasks take 100, 10, 10, 10, 10 and 10 ms. Compared with mapWithLimit(items, 3, task), what happens?
options: Both take the same time, about 100 ms, because both of them keep exactly 3 tasks running at all times
Chunks are faster, about 60 ms, because one Promise.all per chunk has less overhead than a pool of workers
Chunks start all 6 tasks at once, because Promise.all is called before the loop waits
Each chunk waits for its slowest task (120 ms in total, measured); the pool refills slots and took 101 ms
explain: With chunks, the 10 ms tasks of the second chunk wait for the 100 ms task of the first. Measured on Node 24: about 120 ms for the chunks, 101 ms for the pool. Both respect the limit, which is why they look equivalent, but only the pool refills a slot as soon as it frees.

q: Remove the guard on limit from mapWithLimit, then call it with three orders and a limit of 0. What happens?
options: It runs the tasks one at a time, because Math.min falls back to a single worker
It resolves with an array of 3 empty slots, without calling the task once
It never settles, because no worker is ever started to drain the shared iterator
It throws a RangeError from Array.from, because a length of 0 is not allowed there
explain: Math.min(0, 3) starts zero workers, Promise.all([]) fulfils at once, and the pre-sized results array comes back with 3 holes (checked on Node 24). That silent success is worse than an error, which is why the function validates the limit first.

q: Your curry calls the function once it has received fn.length arguments. The interviewer curries function orderTotal(amount, shipping = 499, discount) {…}. What does curry(orderTotal)(4500) do?
options: It calls orderTotal at once with only the amount, because orderTotal.length is 1
It returns a function that waits for the shipping and discount arguments, one at a time
It throws a TypeError, because curry cannot read the length of a function with defaults
It calls orderTotal with shipping set to 499 and discount set to 0 by default
explain: Function length counts parameters before the first one with a default value or a rest parameter; on Node 24, ((a, b = 1) => 0).length is 1. So the curried function has all it expects after one argument. A good answer names this and offers an explicit arity parameter.

q: A pull request on the orders table contains this. Which change would you ship?
options: Switch to useLayoutEffect, so the sorted rows are set before the browser paints the table
Add byTotal to the dependency array, so the effect also re-runs when the comparator changes
Drop the state and the effect, and compute orders.toSorted(byTotal) during render
Deep-clone orders with JSON before sorting, so the parent's array is never mutated
explain: Derived data is computed in render: no stale copy, no extra render, and toSorted leaves the parent's array alone. useLayoutEffect hides the flash but keeps the second render, the copy in state and the mutation. A JSON clone fixes only the mutation, at a cost, and breaks types such as Date.

q: The status filter handler is setQuery({ ...query, status }), without page: 0. An agent on page 3 of 45 orders filters to "paid", which matches 15. What do they see?
options: Page 1 of 1 with 15 orders, because React resets state on change
Page 3 of 3 with the same rows
An error thrown by slice
"Page 3 of 1" and an empty table
explain: The page index stays at 2 while only one page exists, so slice(40, 60) returns nothing. Reproduced in jsdom with Testing Library: "Page 3 of 1" and zero rows. Reset the page in the same handler that changes the filter; React never resets state for you, and slice does not throw past the end.

q: The refund dialog is open with showModal() and holds Cancel and Confirm. Focus is on Confirm, and the user presses Tab. What happens in Chromium?
options: Focus moves to the first link of the page behind the dialog, as in normal document order
Focus leaves the buttons for the document itself, then the next Tab returns to Cancel
Nothing happens: the browser disables the Tab key while a modal dialog is open
The dialog closes, because focus leaving its last element counts as a light dismiss
explain: Measured in Chromium with Playwright: Tab from Confirm went to the document, then back to Cancel, and never to the links behind, which are inert. The tempting first option is what happens with a div styled as a modal and no focus handling.

q: After Confirm, the parent sets open to false and the Modal effect calls dialog.close(). Does the onClose prop run?
options: Yes: close fires on every close, Escape or dialog.close(), so keep onClose idempotent
No: the close event fires only when the user closes the dialog with the Escape key
No: React does not dispatch events that are triggered by code running inside an effect
Yes, but only in development, because StrictMode runs the effect a second time
explain: Measured in Chromium: onClose ran once after Escape and once after the parent closed the dialog through the effect. So setting state to false again is harmless, but a side effect such as an analytics event in onClose would fire for both.

q: For the select-all checkbox, a candidate writes <input type="checkbox" checked={allSelected} indeterminate={someSelected} onChange={toggleAll} />. What happens with React 19.3.1?
options: The checkbox shows the mixed state whenever some orders are selected, and the full state when all are
React writes an indeterminate attribute to the DOM, and the browser reads it to draw the mixed state
TypeScript accepts the prop, and React sets the property after hydration, so it works only on the client
React warns and the property stays false; set input.indeterminate in a ref callback
explain: indeterminate is a DOM property with no HTML attribute. In jsdom with React 19.3.1, the prop logged a warning and the property stayed false, and TypeScript rejects the prop. A ref callback that sets input.indeterminate made the property true.

q: Your MSW test of the error state times out, though the component shows the error in the browser after a few seconds. What is the most likely cause?
options: MSW cannot return a 503 status from a handler, so the request hangs until the test times out
findByRole does not wait for asynchronous updates, so it fails before the error state appears
The test client keeps the default of 3 retries with exponential backoff before the error shows
fetch rejects on a 503 status, so the error is thrown outside React and never reaches the component
explain: The TanStack Query documentation lists 3 retries with exponential backoff as a default; a test client with retry: false shows the error at once. fetch does not reject on a 503 (only on network failure), which is why fetchOrders checks response.ok. findByRole does wait, but only about a second by default.

q: You have 5 minutes left in the review of OrderNotes and have found every issue. In which order do you present them?
options: The missing key first, because it is the only problem that React itself reports in the console
User text rendered as HTML first, as a blocker; then accessibility and correctness; the effect last
Style and naming first, to build rapport, then the bugs in the order you found them
In the order they appear in the file, so the author can follow along line by line
explain: Severity decides: user text rendered as HTML is script injection in an agent's session, so it blocks the merge. Accessibility and correctness issues follow, and the extra render is a suggestion. Leading with the console warning or with file order buries the one finding that matters most.

q: On the storefront, elementFromPoint at the Pay button returns div.toast-region, an empty container fixed over the whole page with a high z-index. Which fix would you ship?
options: Give the region pointer-events: none, and pointer-events: auto to the toasts inside it
Raise the Pay button's z-index above the toast region, so that it is on top again
Add a click handler on the toast region that forwards the click to the pay function
Remove aria-live from the region, because live regions capture pointer events in Chromium
explain: Measured in Chromium: with pointer-events: none on the region, the same mouse click reached the button. Raising one button's z-index fixes only that button and leaves every other control covered; forwarding clicks is a hack. aria-live does not affect hit-testing.

q: After your orders table works, the interviewer asks: "Why did you not just use a table library?" What is the best answer?
options: Libraries are always slower than hand-written code, so I avoid them for anything on a hot path like a table
Serious companies do not allow third-party UI libraries in production because of supply-chain risk
I prefer to own all the code I ship, so I would write and maintain our own table at work as well
The round asked me to build it; at work I would use a headless table library and server-side sorting for large data
explain: A senior separates the exercise from the job: building it by hand shows the skill, and choosing a maintained library at work shows judgement. The other answers state preferences or false generalisations instead of trade-offs, and invite a follow-up you cannot win.
